{{Short description|Digital asset using a distributed ledger}}
{{Distinguish|Virtual currency}}
{{protection padlock|small=yes}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=January 2026}}
{{Use American English|date=January 2026}}

'''Cryptocurrency''' is a type of [[digital asset]] that uses [[distributed ledger]], or [[blockchain]], technology to enable a secure transaction.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Härdle |first1=Wolfgang Karl |last2=Harvey |first2=Campbell R. |last3=Reule |first3=Raphael C. G. |title=Understanding Cryptocurrencies |journal=Journal of Financial Econometrics |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=181–208 |date=2020 |doi=10.1093/jjfinec/nbz033}}</ref>

Individual coin ownership records are stored in a digital ledger or [[blockchain]], which is a computerized [[database]] that uses a consensus mechanism to secure [[E-commerce|transaction]] records, control the creation of additional coins, and verify the transfer of coin ownership.<ref name="crypto currency">{{Cite news |last=Andy Greenberg |date=20 April 2011 |title=Crypto Currency |work=Forbes |url=https://www.forbes.com/forbes/2011/0509/technology-psilocybin-bitcoins-gavin-andresen-crypto-currency.html |url-status=live |access-date=8 August 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140831001109/http://www.forbes.com/forbes/2011/0509/technology-psilocybin-bitcoins-gavin-andresen-crypto-currency.html |archive-date=31 August 2014}}</ref><ref name="reuterspricing">{{Cite news |last=Polansek |first=Tom |date=2 May 2016 |title=CME, ICE prepare pricing data that could boost bitcoin |work=[[Reuters]] |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-cme-group-bitcoin-idUSKCN0XT1G1 |access-date=3 May 2016 |archive-date=23 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220423185213/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-cme-group-bitcoin-idUSKCN0XT1G1 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Pernice|first1=Ingolf G. A.|last2=Scott|first2=Brett|date=20 May 2021|title=Cryptocurrency|url=https://policyreview.info/glossary/cryptocurrency|journal=Internet Policy Review|language=en|volume=10|issue=2|doi=10.14763/2021.2.1561|issn=2197-6775|doi-access=free|access-date=23 October 2021|archive-date=23 October 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211023191023/https://policyreview.info/glossary/cryptocurrency|url-status=live|hdl=10419/235962|hdl-access=free}}</ref> The two most common consensus mechanisms are [[proof of work]] and [[proof of stake]].<ref>{{cite book | last1=Nicolini | first1=Gianni | last2=Intini | first2=Silvia | title=The Cryptocurrency Phenomenon | publisher=Taylor & Francis | publication-place=Abingdon, Oxon New York, NY |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=Y7zHEAAAQBAJ&pg=PT53 | date=16 August 2023 | isbn=978-1-000-92384-1 | page=53|language=en-US}}</ref> Despite the name, which has come to describe many of the [[fungibility|fungible]] blockchain tokens that have been created, cryptocurrencies are not considered to be [[Currency|currencies]] in the traditional sense, and varying legal treatments have been applied to them in various jurisdictions, including classification as [[Commodity|commodities]], [[Security (finance)|securities]], and currencies. Cryptocurrencies are generally viewed as a distinct asset class in practice.<ref>{{Cite news|date=7 March 2014|title=Bitcoin not a currency says Japan government|language=en-GB|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-26478059|access-date=25 January 2022|archive-date=25 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220125102155/https://www.bbc.com/news/business-26478059|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|date=3 March 2020|title=Is it a currency? A commodity? Bitcoin has an identity crisis|language=en|work=Reuters|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-crypto-currencies-idUSKBN20Q0LK|access-date=25 January 2022|archive-date=25 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220125102143/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-crypto-currencies-idUSKBN20Q0LK|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Brown|first=Aaron|date=7 November 2017|title=Are Cryptocurrencies an Asset Class? Yes and No|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/articles/2017-11-07/are-cryptocurrencies-an-asset-class-yes-and-no|access-date=25 January 2022|website=www.bloomberg.com|archive-date=1 April 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220401021540/https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/articles/2017-11-07/are-cryptocurrencies-an-asset-class-yes-and-no|url-status=live}}</ref>

==History==
{{Further|History of bitcoin|Cryptocurrency bubble#History}}

In 1983, American [[Cryptography|cryptographer]] [[David Chaum]] conceived of a type of cryptographic [[electronic money]] called [[ecash]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Chaum |first=David |author-link=David Chaum |date=2013 |orig-date=1983 |chapter=Blind Signatures for Untraceable Payments |editor=David Chaum |title=Advances in Cryptology: Proceedings of Crypto 82 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-1475706048 |via=www.hit.bme.hu |chapter-url=http://www.hit.bme.hu/~buttyan/courses/BMEVIHIM219/2009/Chaum.BlindSigForPayment.1982.PDF |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141218034712/http://www.hit.bme.hu/%7Ebuttyan/courses/BMEVIHIM219/2009/Chaum.BlindSigForPayment.1982.PDF |archive-date=18 December 2014 |access-date=26 October 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Chaum |first1=David |author1-link=David Chaum |last2=Fiat |first2=Amos |last3=Naor |first3=Moni |date=1990 |chapter=Untraceable Electronic Cash |editor=Shafi Goldwasser |title=Advances in Cryptology - CRYPTO '88: Proceedings |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-0387971964 |via=blog.koehntopp.de |chapter-url=http://blog.koehntopp.de/uploads/chaum_fiat_naor_ecash.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110903023027/http://blog.koehntopp.de/uploads/chaum_fiat_naor_ecash.pdf |archive-date=3 September 2011 |access-date=10 October 2012 }}</ref> Later, in 1995, he implemented it through [[Digicash]],<ref>{{cite web |last=Pitta |first=Julie |title=Requiem for a Bright Idea |website=[[Forbes]] |url=https://www.forbes.com/forbes/1999/1101/6411390a.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170830214226/https://www.forbes.com/forbes/1999/1101/6411390a.html |archive-date=30 August 2017 |access-date=11 January 2018}}</ref> an early form of cryptographic electronic payments. Digicash required user software in order to withdraw notes from a bank and designate specific encrypted keys before they could be sent to a recipient. This allowed the digital currency to be untraceable by a third party.

In 1996, the [[National Security Agency]] published a paper entitled ''How to Make a Mint: The Cryptography of Anonymous Electronic Cash'', describing a cryptocurrency system. The paper was first published in an [[MIT]] mailing list (October 1996) and later (April 1997) in ''The American Law Review''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Law |first1=Laurie |last2=Sabett |first2=Susan |last3=Solinas |first3=Jerry |date=April 1997 |title=How to Make a Mint: The Cryptography of Anonymous Electronic Cash |journal=The American University Law Review |volume=46 |issue=4 |url=http://digitalcommons.wcl.american.edu/aulr/vol46/iss4/6/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180112043050/http://digitalcommons.wcl.american.edu/aulr/vol46/iss4/6/ |archive-date=12 January 2018 |access-date=11 January 2018 }}</ref>

In 1998, [[Wei Dai]] described "b-money," an anonymous, distributed electronic cash system.<ref>{{cite web |last=Wei Dai |year=1998 |title=B-Money |url=http://www.weidai.com/bmoney.txt |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111105071114/http://www.weidai.com/bmoney.txt |archive-date=5 November 2011 |publisher=www.weidai.com}}</ref> Shortly thereafter, [[Nick Szabo]] described [[bit gold]].<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Peck |first=Morgen E. |date=30 May 2012 |title=Bitcoin: The Cryptoanarchists' Answer to Cash |url=https://spectrum.ieee.org/bitcoin-the-cryptoanarchists-answer-to-cash |magazine=[[IEEE Spectrum]] |quote=Around the same time, Nick Szabo, a computer scientist who now blogs about law and the history of money, was one of the first to imagine a new digital currency from the ground up. Although many consider his scheme, which he calls 'bit gold', to be a precursor to Bitcoin... |access-date=2 February 2020 |archive-date=21 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191221171012/https://spectrum.ieee.org/computing/software/bitcoin-the-cryptoanarchists-answer-to-cash |url-status=live }}</ref> Like bitcoin and other later cryptocurrencies, bit gold was proposed as a digital currency system in which users would generate money by completing proof-of-work functions whose solutions were cryptographically chained and published.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Narayanan |first1=Arvind |last2=Clark |first2=Jeremy |date=29 August 2017 |title=Bitcoin's Academic Pedigree |url=https://queue.acm.org/detail.cfm?id=3136559 |magazine=ACM Queue |volume=15 |issue=4 |publisher=Association for Computing Machinery |access-date=23 April 2026}}</ref>

In January 2009, bitcoin was created by [[pseudonym]]ous developer [[Satoshi Nakamoto]]. It used [[SHA-256]], a cryptographic hash function, in its [[proof-of-work]] scheme.<ref name="primer" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Niccolai |first=James |date=19 May 2013 |title=Bitcoin developer chats about regulation, open source, and the elusive Satoshi Nakamoto |url=https://www.pcworld.com/article/451943/bitcoin-developer-talks-regulation-open-source-and-the-elusive-satoshi-nakamoto.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141003104345/http://www.pcworld.com/article/2039184/bitcoin-developer-talks-regulation-open-source-and-the-elusive-satoshi-nakamoto.html |archive-date=3 October 2014 |access-date=17 August 2022 |website=PCWorld |language=en-US}}</ref> In April 2011, [[Namecoin]] was created as an attempt at forming a decentralized [[domain name system|DNS]]. In October 2011, [[Litecoin]] was released, which used [[scrypt]] as its hash function instead of SHA-256. [[Peercoin]], created in August 2012, used a hybrid of proof-of-work and [[proof-of-stake]].<ref name=Steadman2013>{{Cite web |last=Steadman |first=Ian |date=11 May 2013 |title=Wary of Bitcoin? A guide to some other cryptocurrencies |website=Ars Technica |url=https://arstechnica.com/information-technology/2013/05/wary-of-bitcoin-a-guide-to-some-other-cryptocurrencies/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140116040533/http://arstechnica.com/business/2013/05/wary-of-bitcoin-a-guide-to-some-other-cryptocurrencies/ |archive-date=16 January 2014 |access-date=17 August 2022 }}</ref>

Cryptocurrency has undergone several periods of growth and retraction, including several [[Economic bubble|bubbles]] and market crashes, such as in 2011, 2013–2014/15, 2017–2018, and 2021–2023.<ref>{{Cite news |title='Crypto winter' has come. And it's looking more like an ice age |newspaper=The Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2022/12/18/crypto-winter-ftx-collapse-bitcoin-prices/ |access-date=13 April 2023 |issn=0190-8286 |archive-date=29 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221229181753/https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2022/12/18/crypto-winter-ftx-collapse-bitcoin-prices/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=What Is Crypto Winter? |department=Forbes Advisor |url=https://www.forbes.com/advisor/investing/cryptocurrency/what-is-crypto-winter/ |access-date=13 April 2023 |website=Forbes |archive-date=13 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230413220125/https://www.forbes.com/advisor/investing/cryptocurrency/what-is-crypto-winter/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In August 2014, the UK announced its [[HM Treasury|Treasury]] had commissioned a study of cryptocurrencies and what role, if any, they could play in the UK economy. The study was also to report on whether regulation should be considered.<ref name="Crypto currencyUK">{{Cite news |date=7 August 2014 |title=UK launches initiative to explore potential of virtual currencies |publisher=The UK News |url=http://www.theuknews.com/index.php/sid/224504231 |url-status=live |access-date=8 August 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141110202812/http://www.theuknews.com/index.php/sid/224504231 |archive-date=10 November 2014}}</ref> Its final report was published in 2018,<ref>{{cite web |date=October 2018 |title=Cryptoassets Taskforce: final report |url=https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/752070/cryptoassets_taskforce_final_report_final_web.pdf |access-date=1 October 2021 |website=assets.publishing.service.gov.uk |publisher=HM Treasury |archive-date=23 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210923211025/https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/752070/cryptoassets_taskforce_final_report_final_web.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> and it issued a consultation on cryptoassets and [[stablecoin]]s in January 2021.<ref>{{cite web |title=UK regulatory approach to cryptoassets and stablecoins: Consultation and call for evidence |url=https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/950206/HM_Treasury_Cryptoasset_and_Stablecoin_consultation.pdf |publisher=HM Treasury |access-date=1 October 2021 |archive-date=25 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221125202157/https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment_data/file/950206/HM_Treasury_Cryptoasset_and_Stablecoin_consultation.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

In June 2021, [[El Salvador]] became the first country to accept bitcoin as [[legal tender]], after the [[Legislative Assembly of El Salvador|Legislative Assembly]] had voted 62–22 to pass a bill submitted by President [[Nayib Bukele]] classifying the cryptocurrency as such.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://en.mercopress.com/2021/06/10/bitcoin-legal-tender-in-el-salvador-first-country-ever |title=Bitcoin legal tender in El Salvador, first country ever |website=Mercopress |date=10 June 2021 |access-date=11 June 2021 |archive-date=17 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230217114607/https://en.mercopress.com/2021/06/10/bitcoin-legal-tender-in-el-salvador-first-country-ever |url-status=live }}</ref>

In August 2021, [[Cuba]] followed with Resolution 215 to recognize and regulate cryptocurrencies such as bitcoin.<ref>{{cite web |last=Sigalos |first=MacKenzie |date=27 August 2021 |title=Cuba's central bank now recognizes cryptocurrencies such as bitcoin |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/08/27/cubas-central-bank-now-recognizes-cryptocurrencies-like-bitcoin.html |publisher=CNBC |access-date=6 September 2021 |archive-date=17 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230217114606/https://www.cnbc.com/2021/08/27/cubas-central-bank-now-recognizes-cryptocurrencies-like-bitcoin.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

In September 2021, the [[government of China]], the single largest market for cryptocurrency, declared all cryptocurrency transactions illegal. This completed a crackdown on cryptocurrency that had previously banned the operation of intermediaries and miners within China.<ref name="BBC News">{{Cite news|date=24 September 2021|title=China declares all crypto-currency transactions illegal|language=en-GB|publisher=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-58678907|access-date=24 September 2021|archive-date=17 February 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230217120109/https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-58678907|url-status=live}}</ref>

In September 2022, the world's second largest cryptocurrency at that time, [[Ethereum]], transitioned its [[Consensus (computer science)|consensus mechanism]] from [[Proof of work|proof-of-work]] (PoW) to [[Proof of stake|proof-of-stake]] (PoS) in an upgrade process known as "the Merge".  According to the Ethereum Founder, the upgrade would cut both Ethereum's energy use and carbon-dioxide emissions by 99.9%.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-09-15/ethereum-completes-long-awaited-energy-saving-merge-upgrade|title=Ethereum Finishes Long-Awaited Energy-Saving 'Merge' Upgrade |date=15 September 2022 |publisher=Bloomberg News}}</ref>

On 11 November 2022, [[FTX Trading Ltd.]], a [[cryptocurrency exchange]], which also operated a crypto [[hedge fund]], and had been valued at $18 billion,<ref name=valued>{{Cite news|last=Osipovich|first=Alexander|date=20 July 2017|title=Crypto Exchange FTX Valued at $18 Billion in Funding Round|language=en-US|work=[[The Wall Street Journal]]|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/crypto-exchange-ftx-valued-at-18-billion-in-funding-round-11626800455|access-date=28 December 2022|issn=0099-9660|archive-date=18 November 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221118075444/https://www.wsj.com/articles/crypto-exchange-ftx-valued-at-18-billion-in-funding-round-11626800455|url-status=live}}</ref> [[bankruptcy |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-11-11/ftx-com-goes-bankrupt-in-stunning-reversal-for-crypto-exchange |access-date=28 December 2022 |publisher=[[Bloomberg News]] |date=11 November 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230111122757/https://www.wired.com/story/the-fallout-of-the-ftx-collapse/|url-status=live}}</ref> while, at a [[Reuters]] conference, financial industry executives said that "regulators must step in to protect crypto investors."<ref name=protect>{{cite news|last1=Chatterjee|first1=Sumeet|last2=Davies|first2=Megan|last3=Aftab|first3=Ahmed|last4=McCrank|first4=John|last5=Nguyen|first5=Lananh|last6=Howcroft|first6=Elizabeth|last7=Azhar|first7=Saeed|last8=Sinclair }}</ref>

An October 2024 survey from the [[Pew Research Center]] found that 63% of adults in the U.S. "have little to no confidence that current ways to invest in, trade or use cryptocurrencies are reliable and safe." The survey also reported that 17% of U.S. adults had directly interacted with cryptocurrency, which was statistically unchanged from 2021.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Faverio |first1=Michelle |last2=Dawson |first2=Wyatt |last3=Sidoti |first3=Olivia |title=Majority of Americans aren't confident in the safety and reliability of cryptocurrency |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/10/24/majority-of-americans-arent-confident-in-the-safety-and-reliability-of-cryptocurrency/ |website=[[Pew Research Center]] |access-date=8 March 2025 |date=24 October 2024}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Perrin |first1=Andrew |title=16% of Americans say they have ever invested in, traded or used cryptocurrency |url=https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2021/11/11/16-of-americans-say-they-have-ever-invested-in-traded-or-used-cryptocurrency/ |website=Pew Research Center |access-date=23 November 2025 |date=11 November 2021}}</ref>

==Terminology==
[[File:Bitcoin.svg|thumb|183x183px|A logo for [[bitcoin]], the largest cryptocurrency]]

The word "cryptocurrency", in its modern sense, was added to the [[Oxford English Dictionary]] in September 2018, with its earliest usage noted as being on [[Twitter]] in September 2009;<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.oed.com/dictionary/cryptocurrency_n?tab=meaning_and_use#1264092500|title=Oxford English Dictionary}}</ref> its [[diminutive]], ''crypto'', was entered in 2022.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.oed.com/dictionary/crypto_n3?tab=compounds_and_derived_words&view=curated#1368484010|title=cryptocurrency, n. meanings, etymology and more &#124; Oxford English Dictionary}}</ref>       In March 2018 ''cryptocurrency'' was added to the ''[[Merriam-Webster Dictionary]]''.<ref>{{cite web |date=March 2018 |title=The Dictionary Just Got a Whole Lot Bigger |url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/words-at-play/new-words-in-the-dictionary-march-2018 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180305144056/https://www.merriam-webster.com/words-at-play/new-words-in-the-dictionary-march-2018 |archive-date=5 March 2018 |access-date=5 March 2018 |website=Merriam-Webster}}</ref>

===Altcoins===
{{further|List of cryptocurrencies}}

After the early innovation of bitcoin in 2008 and the early [[network effect]] gained by bitcoin, tokens, cryptocurrencies, and other digital assets that were not bitcoin became collectively known during the 2010s as alternative cryptocurrencies,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/want-to-keep-up-with-bitcoin-enthusiasts-learn-the-lingo-1517394601|title=Want to Keep Up With Bitcoin Enthusiasts? A [[Polytechnic University of Catalonia]] thesis in 2021 used a broader description, including not only alternative versions of bitcoin but every cryptocurrency other than bitcoin. As of early 2020, there were more than 5,000 cryptocurrencies.

Altcoins often have underlying differences when compared to bitcoin. For example, [[Litecoin]] aims to process a block every 2.5 minutes, rather than bitcoin's 10 minutes which allows Litecoin to confirm transactions faster than bitcoin.{{r|Steadman2013}} Another [[Meme coin|Memecoins]] are a category of cryptocurrencies that originated from [[Internet meme]]s or jokes. One example is [[Dogecoin]], a memecoin featuring the [[Shiba Inu]] dog from the [[Doge (meme)|Doge]] meme.<ref name=Yaffe-Bellany>David Yaffe-Bellany, [https://www.nytimes.com/2024/07/27/technology/memecoins-crypto-surge.html A Digital Coin Based on Baby Trump? Yup.], ''New York Times'' (27 July 2024).</ref> Donald Trump and his wife [[Melania Trump|Melania]] are the subject of their own meme coins, both of which declined in value soon after launch.<ref name=CBS_20250424/><ref name=CNBC_20250506/>

Memecoins are known for extreme volatility; for example, the record-high value for a Dogecoin was 73 cents, but that had plunged to 13 cents by mid-2024.<ref name=Yaffe-Bellany/> Scams are prolific among memecoins.<ref name=Yaffe-Bellany/>

==Physical crypto==
[[File:Bit-coin.jpg|thumb|160px|Physical bitcoin]]
Physical cryptocurrency coins have been made as promotional items and some have become collectibles.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Staff |first=Numismatic News |date=23 June 2023 |title=Physical Cryptocurrency Sells Big at Auction |url=https://www.numismaticnews.net/world-coins/physical-cryptocurrency-sells-big-at-auction |access-date=9 June 2024 |website=Numismatic News |language=en |archive-date=9 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240609130325/https://www.numismaticnews.net/world-coins/physical-cryptocurrency-sells-big-at-auction |url-status=live }}</ref> Some of these have a private key embedded in them to access crypto worth a few dollars. There have also been attempts to issue bitcoin "bank notes".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Giedroyc |first=Richard |date=20 February 2024 |title=Promoting Physical Cryptocurrency |url=https://www.numismaticnews.net/paper-money/promoting-physical-cryptocurrency |access-date=9 June 2024 |website=Numismatic News |language=en |archive-date=9 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240609125954/https://www.numismaticnews.net/paper-money/promoting-physical-cryptocurrency |url-status=live }}</ref>

The term "physical bitcoin" is used in the finance industry when investment funds that hold crypto purchased from crypto exchanges put their crypto holdings in a specialised bank called a "custodian".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Coles-Andrew |first=Graeme |date=19 January 2024 |title=WisdomTree cuts fees on its European Physical Bitcoin ETP |url=https://www.thearmchairtrader.com/wisdomtree-europe-physical-bitcoin-etp-etf/ |access-date=9 June 2024 |website=The Armchair Trader |language=en-GB |archive-date=9 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240609130325/https://www.thearmchairtrader.com/wisdomtree-europe-physical-bitcoin-etp-etf/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

These physical representations of cryptocurrency do not hold any value by themselves; these are only utilized for collectable purposes. For example, the first incarnation of the bitcoin Casascius, coins made of silver, brass or aluminum sometimes with gold plating, or Titan Bitcoin, which in silver or gold versions are sought after by [[numismatist]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Casascius, Titan physical bitcoins give numismatic identity |url=https://www.coinworld.com/news/paper-money/bitcoin-coin-world-virtual-currency-titan-bitcoin-casascius-physical-bitcoin-numismatics-coin-collecting.html |access-date=19 April 2025 |website=CoinWorld |language=en}}</ref>

==Architecture==
{{Duplication|date=August 2022|dupe=Blockchain|section}}

The underlying technical system upon which cryptocurrencies are based was created by [[Satoshi Nakamoto]].<ref name="te20151031">{{Cite news |date=31 October 2015 |title=Blockchains: The great chain of being sure about things |url=https://www.economist.com/news/briefing/21677228-technology-behind-bitcoin-lets-people-who-do-not-know-or-trust-each-other-build-dependable |url-status=live |newspaper=[[The Economist]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160703000844/http://www.economist.com/news/briefing/21677228-technology-behind-bitcoin-lets-people-who-do-not-know-or-trust-each-other-build-dependable |archive-date=3 July 2016 |access-date=18 June 2016}}</ref>

Within a [[proof-of-work]] system such as bitcoin, the safety, integrity, and balance of [[ledger]]s are maintained by a community of mutually distrustful parties referred to as [[Bitcoin miners|miners]]. Miners use their computers to help validate and timestamp transactions, adding them to the ledger in accordance with a particular timestamping scheme.<ref name="primer">{{cite web |last=Jerry Brito and Andrea Castillo |year=2013 |title=Bitcoin: A Primer for Policymakers |url=http://mercatus.org/sites/default/files/Brito_BitcoinPrimer.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130921060724/http://mercatus.org/sites/default/files/Brito_BitcoinPrimer.pdf |archive-date=21 September 2013 |access-date=22 October 2013 |website=Mercatus Center |publisher=George Mason University}}</ref> In a [[proof-of-stake]] blockchain, transactions are validated by holders of the associated cryptocurrency, sometimes grouped together in stake pools.

Most cryptocurrencies are designed to gradually decrease the production of that currency, placing a cap on the total amount of that currency that will ever be in circulation.<ref>"[http://www.americanbanker.com/bankthink/how-cryptocurrencies-could-upend-banks-monetary-role-1057597-1.html?zkPrintable=1&nopagination=1 How Cryptocurrencies Could Upend Banks' Monetary Role]". {{webarchive |url= https://web.archive.org/web/20130927084451/http://www.americanbanker.com/bankthink/how-cryptocurrencies-could-upend-banks-monetary-role-1057597-1.html?zkPrintable=1&nopagination=1 |date=27 September 2013 }}, ''American Banker''. 26 May 2013</ref> Compared with ordinary currencies held by financial institutions or kept as [[cash]] on hand, cryptocurrencies can be more difficult for [[Search and seizure|seizure]] by law enforcement.<ref name="crypto currency" />

===Blockchain===
{{Main|Blockchain}}

The validity of each cryptocurrency's coins is provided by a [[blockchain]]. A blockchain is a continuously growing list of [[Record (computer science)|records]], called ''blocks'', which are linked and secured using cryptography.<ref name="te20151031" /><ref name="cryptocurrencytech">{{Cite book |last1=Narayanan |first1=Arvind |title=Bitcoin and cryptocurrency technologies: a comprehensive introduction |last2=Bonneau |first2=Joseph |last3=Felten |first3=Edward |last4=Miller |first4=Andrew |last5=Goldfeder |first5=Steven |date=2016 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-17169-2 |location=Princeton}}</ref> Each block typically contains a [[Cryptographic hash function|hash]] pointer as a link to a previous block,<ref name="cryptocurrencytech" /> a [[Trusted timestamping|timestamp]], and transaction data.<ref name="IPblockchain">{{cite web |title=Blockchain |url=http://www.investopedia.com/terms/b/blockchain.asp |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160323045814/http://www.investopedia.com/terms/b/blockchain.asp |archive-date=23 March 2016 |access-date=19 March 2016 |website=Investopedia |quote=Based on the Bitcoin protocol, the blockchain database is shared by all nodes participating in a system.}}</ref> By design, blockchains are inherently resistant to modification of the data. A blockchain is "an open, [[distributed ledger]] that can record transactions between two parties efficiently and in a verifiable and permanent way".<ref name="hbr201701">{{Cite news |last1=Iansiti |first1=Marco |last2=Lakhani |first2=Karim R. |date=January 2017 |title=The Truth About Blockchain |work=[[Harvard Business Review]] |publisher=[[Harvard University]] |url=https://hbr.org/2017/01/the-truth-about-blockchain |url-status=live |access-date=17 January 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170118052537/https://hbr.org/2017/01/the-truth-about-blockchain |archive-date=18 January 2017 |quote=The technology at the heart of bitcoin and other virtual currencies, blockchain is an open, distributed ledger that can record transactions between two parties efficiently and in a verifiable and permanent way.}}</ref>

For use as a distributed ledger, a blockchain is typically managed by a [[peer-to-peer]] network collectively adhering to a protocol for validating new blocks. Once recorded, the data in any given block cannot be altered retroactively without the alteration of all subsequent blocks, which requires collusion of the network majority.

Blockchains are [[secure by design]] and are an example of a distributed computing system with high [[Byzantine fault tolerance]]. [[Decentralized]] consensus has therefore been achieved with a blockchain.<ref name="decapp">{{Cite book |last=Raval |first=Siraj |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fvywDAAAQBAJ |title=Decentralized Applications: Harnessing Bitcoin's Blockchain Technology |publisher=O'Reilly Media, Inc. |year=2016 |isbn=978-1-4919-2452-5 |pages=[{{google books|fvywDAAAQBAJ|page=1|plainurl=yes}} 1]–[{{google books |chapter=What Is a Decentralized Application? |oclc=968277125 |access-date=6 November 2016 |chapter-url={{google books|fvywDAAAQBAJ|page=1|plainurl=yes}} |via=Google Books |fvywDAAAQBAJ |plainurl=yes}} 2] |access-date=21 January 2018 |archive-date=28 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240628094550/https://books.google.com/books?id=fvywDAAAQBAJ |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Nodes===
A "node" is a computer that connects to a cryptocurrency network. The node supports the cryptocurrency's network through either relaying transactions, validation, or hosting a copy of the blockchain. In terms of relaying transactions, each network computer (node) has a copy of the blockchain of the cryptocurrency it supports. When a transaction is made, the node creating the transaction broadcasts details of the transaction using encryption to other nodes throughout the node network so that the transaction (and every other transaction) is known.

Node owners are either volunteers, those hosted by the organization or body developing the technology, or those incentivised by rewards from the node network.<ref>{{Cite journal|doi = 10.1109/ACCESS.2019.2914098|title = Nodes in the Bitcoin Network: Comparative Measurement Study and Survey|year = 2019|last1 = Park|first1 = Sehyun|last2 = Im|first2 = Seongwon|last3 = Seol|first3 = Youhwan|last4 = Paek|first4 = Jeongyeup|journal = IEEE Access|volume = 7|pages = 57009–57022| bibcode=2019IEEEA...757009P |s2cid = 155106629|doi-access = free}}</ref>

====Timestamping====
Cryptocurrencies use various timestamping schemes to "prove" the validity of transactions added to the blockchain ledger without the need for a trusted third party.

The first timestamping scheme invented was the [[Proof of work|proof-of-work]] scheme. The most widely used proof-of-work schemes are based on SHA-256 and [[scrypt]].{{r|Steadman2013}}

Some other hashing algorithms that are used for proof-of-work include [[CryptoNote]], [[BLAKE (hash function)|Blake]], [[SHA-3]], and [[X11 algorithm|X11]].

Another method is called the [[Proof of stake|proof-of-stake]] scheme. Proof-of-stake is a method of securing a cryptocurrency network and achieving distributed consensus through requesting users to show ownership of a certain amount of currency. It is different from proof-of-work systems that run difficult hashing algorithms to validate electronic transactions. The scheme is largely dependent on the coin, and there is currently no standard form of it. Some cryptocurrencies use a combined proof-of-work and proof-of-stake scheme.{{r|Steadman2013}}

===Mining===
{{See also|GPU mining}}
[[File:Оборудование HashCoins.jpg|thumb|A hashcoin [[Bitcoin network#Mining|mine]]]]

On a blockchain, ''mining'' is the validation of transactions. For this effort, successful miners obtain new cryptocurrency as a reward. The reward decreases [[#Transaction fees|transaction fees]] by creating a complementary incentive to contribute to the processing power of the network. The rate of generating hashes, which validate any transaction, has been increased by the use of specialized hardware such as [[Field-programmable gate array|FPGA]]s and [[Application-specific integrated circuit|ASIC]]s running complex hashing algorithms like SHA-256 and [[scrypt]].<ref name=computer201709>{{Cite magazine|title=The Evolution of Bitcoin Hardware|date=1 September 2017|magazine=Computer|url=https://www.computer.org/csdl/magazine/co/2017/09/mco2017090058/13rRUwghdcJ|last=Bedford Taylor|first=Michael|access-date=14 December 2020|archive-date=27 September 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200927165421/https://www.computer.org/csdl/magazine/co/2017/09/mco2017090058/13rRUwghdcJ|url-status=live}}</ref> This arms race for cheaper-yet-efficient machines has existed since bitcoin was introduced in 2009.<ref name=computer201709 /> Mining is measured by [[Hashrate|hash rate]], typically in TH/s.<ref>{{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HWJ6EAAAQBAJ&dq=Crypto+mining+th%2Fs&pg=PA222 | title=Cryptocurrency Mining for Dummies | isbn=9781119885368 | last1=Kent | first1=Peter | last2=Bain | first2=Tyler | date=13 July 2022 | publisher=John Wiley & Sons | access-date=7 February 2023 | archive-date=28 June 2024 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240628094521/https://books.google.com/books?id=HWJ6EAAAQBAJ&dq=Crypto+mining+th%2Fs&pg=PA222#v=onepage&q=Crypto%20mining%20th%2Fs&f=false | url-status=live }}</ref> A 2023 [[IMF]] working paper found that crypto mining could generate 450 million tons of {{CO2}} emissions by 2027, accounting for 0.7 percent of global emissions, or 1.2 percent of the world total.<ref>{{Cite news |date=15 August 2024 |title=Carbon Emissions from AI and Crypto Are Surging and Tax Policy Can Help |work= IMF |url=https://www.imf.org/en/Blogs/Articles/2024/08/15/carbon-emissions-from-ai-and-crypto-are-surging-and-tax-policy-can-help|access-date=27 October 2024}}</ref>

With more people entering the world of virtual currency, generating hashes for validation has become more complex over time, forcing miners to invest increasingly large sums of money to improve computing performance. Consequently, the reward for finding a hash has diminished and often does not justify the investment in equipment and cooling facilities (to mitigate the heat the equipment produces) and the electricity required to run them.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Hern |first=Alex |date=17 January 2018 |title=Bitcoin's energy usage is huge – we can't afford to ignore it |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2018/jan/17/bitcoin-electricity-usage-huge-climate-cryptocurrency |url-status=live |access-date=23 January 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180123061505/https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2018/jan/17/bitcoin-electricity-usage-huge-climate-cryptocurrency |archive-date=23 January 2018}}</ref>

Popular regions for mining include those with inexpensive electricity, a cold climate, and jurisdictions with clear and conducive regulations. By July 2019, bitcoin's electricity consumption was estimated to be approximately 7 gigawatts, around 0.2% of the global total, or equivalent to the energy consumed nationally by Switzerland.<ref>{{cite web |last=Baraniuk |first=Chris |date=3 July 2019 |title=Bitcoin's global energy use 'equals Switzerland' |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-48853230 |access-date=2 February 2020 |website=BBC News |archive-date=16 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200116160730/https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-48853230 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Some [[Mining pool|miners pool resources]], sharing their [[computer performance|processing power]] over a network to split the reward equally, according to the amount of work they contributed to the probability of finding a [[blockchain (database)|block]]. A "share" is awarded to members of the mining pool who present a valid partial proof-of-work.

{{As of|2018|02}}, the Chinese government has halted trading of virtual currency, banned initial coin offerings, and shut down mining. Many Chinese miners have since relocated to Canada<ref>{{Cite news |date=2 February 2018 |title=China's Crypto Crackdown Sends Miners Scurrying to Chilly Canada |newspaper=Bloomberg.com |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-02-02/china-crypto-exodus-leads-to-cheap-clean-power-in-chilly-canada |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180304090651/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-02-02/china-crypto-exodus-leads-to-cheap-clean-power-in-chilly-canada |archive-date=4 March 2018 |access-date=3 March 2018 |publisher=Bloomberg L.P.}}</ref> and Texas.<ref>{{Cite news|url = https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-58414555|title = Why China's bitcoin miners are moving to Texas|work = BBC News|date = 3 September 2021|access-date = 4 September 2021|archive-date = 4 September 2021|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210904221716/https://www.bbc.com/news/world-us-canada-58414555|url-status = live}}</ref> One company is operating data centers for mining operations at Canadian oil and gas field sites due to low gas prices.<ref>{{cite web |date=26 January 2018 |title=Cryptocurrency mining operation launched by Iron Bridge Resources |url=http://www.worldoil.com/news/2018/1/26/cryptocurrency-mining-operation-launched-by-iron-bridge-resources |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180130091353/http://www.worldoil.com/news/2018/1/26/cryptocurrency-mining-operation-launched-by-iron-bridge-resources |archive-date=30 January 2018 |website=World Oil}}</ref> In June 2018, [[Hydro-Québec|Hydro Quebec]] proposed to the provincial government to allocate 500 megawatts of power to crypto companies for mining.<ref>{{cite web |title=Bitcoin and crypto currencies trending up today - Crypto Currency Daily Roundup June 25 - Market Exclusive |url=https://marketexclusive.com/bitcoin-major-currencies-today-crypto-currency-daily-roundup-june-25/2018/06/ |access-date=27 June 2018 |website=marketexclusive.com |date=25 June 2018 |archive-date=13 April 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200413024944/https://marketexclusive.com/bitcoin-major-currencies-today-crypto-currency-daily-roundup-june-25/2018/06/ |url-status=live }}</ref> According to a February 2018 report from ''[[Fortune (magazine)|Fortune]]'', Iceland has become a haven for cryptocurrency miners in part because of its cheap electricity.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Iceland Expects to Use More Electricity Mining Bitcoin Than Powering Homes This Year |work=Fortune |url=http://fortune.com/2018/02/13/iceland-bitcoin-mining-electricity/ |url-status=live |access-date=25 March 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180420081336/http://fortune.com/2018/02/13/iceland-bitcoin-mining-electricity/ |archive-date=20 April 2018}}</ref>

In March 2018, the city of [[Plattsburgh (city), New York|Plattsburgh, New York]] put an 18-month [[Moratorium (law)|moratorium]] on all cryptocurrency mining in an effort to preserve natural resources and the "character and direction" of the city.<ref>{{Cite news |date=16 March 2018 |title=Bitcoin Mining Banned for First Time in Upstate New York Town |newspaper=Bloomberg.com |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-03-16/bitcoin-mining-banned-for-first-time-in-upstate-new-york-town |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180320170609/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-03-16/bitcoin-mining-banned-for-first-time-in-upstate-new-york-town |archive-date=20 March 2018 |access-date=20 March 2018 |publisher=Bloomberg L.P.}}</ref> In 2021, [[Kazakhstan]] became the second-biggest crypto-currency mining country, producing 18.1% of the global [[exahash]] rate. The country built a compound containing 50,000 computers near [[Ekibastuz]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/av/technology-60148754 |title=Inside Kazakhstan's giant crypto-mine |website=BBC |date=31 January 2022 |access-date=28 March 2022 |archive-date=28 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220328171928/https://www.bbc.com/news/av/technology-60148754 |url-status=live }}</ref>

====GPU price rise====
An increase in cryptocurrency mining increased the demand for [[graphics cards]] (GPU) in 2017.<ref>{{cite web |title=Bitcoin mania is hurting PC gamers by pushing up GPU prices |date=30 January 2018 |url=https://www.theverge.com/2018/1/30/16949550/bitcoin-graphics-cards-pc-prices-surge |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180202070911/https://www.theverge.com/2018/1/30/16949550/bitcoin-graphics-cards-pc-prices-surge |archive-date=2 February 2018 |access-date=2 February 2018}}</ref> The computing power of GPUs makes them well-suited to generating hashes. Popular favorites of cryptocurrency miners, such as Nvidia's [[GTX 1060]] and [[GTX 1070]] graphics cards, as well as AMD's RX 570 and RX 580 GPUs, doubled or tripled in price{{snd}}or simply went out of stock.<ref>{{cite web |title=Graphics card shortage leads retailers to take unusual measures |website=[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] |date=26 January 2018 |url=https://www.polygon.com/2018/1/26/16936984/graphics-card-gpu-prices-nvidia-amd-cryptocurrency-mining-stores |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180202190305/https://www.polygon.com/2018/1/26/16936984/graphics-card-gpu-prices-nvidia-amd-cryptocurrency-mining-stores |archive-date=2 February 2018 |access-date=2 February 2018}}</ref>

A GTX 1070 Ti, which was released at a price of $450, sold for as much as $1,100. Another popular card, the GTX 1060 (6 GB model), released at an [[MSRP]] of $250, sold for almost $500. RX 570 and RX 580 cards from [[AMD]] were out of stock for almost a year. Miners regularly buy up the entire stock of new GPUs as soon as they are available.<ref>{{cite web |title=AMD, Nvidia must do more to stop cryptominers from causing PC gaming card shortages, price gouging |website=[[CNBC]] |date=22 January 2018 |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2018/01/22/amd-nvidia-must-do-more-to-stop-cryptominers-from-causing-shortages.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180202094859/https://www.cnbc.com/2018/01/22/amd-nvidia-must-do-more-to-stop-cryptominers-from-causing-shortages.html |archive-date=2 February 2018 |access-date=2 February 2018}}</ref>

[[Nvidia]] has asked retailers to do what they can when it comes to selling GPUs to gamers instead of miners. Boris Böhles, PR manager for Nvidia in the German region, said: "Gamers come first for Nvidia."<ref>{{cite web |title=Nvidia suggests retailers put gamers over cryptocurrency miners in graphics card craze |website=[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] |date=23 January 2018 |url=https://www.polygon.com/2018/1/23/16921356/nvidia-graphics-cards-sold-out-cryptocurrency-miners |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180202190249/https://www.polygon.com/2018/1/23/16921356/nvidia-graphics-cards-sold-out-cryptocurrency-miners |archive-date=2 February 2018 |access-date=2 February 2018}}</ref>

====Mining accelerator chips====
Numerous companies developed dedicated crypto-mining accelerator chips, capable of price-performance far higher than that of CPU or [[GPU mining]]. At one point, [[Intel]] marketed its own brand of crypto accelerator chip, named [[Blockscale]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Cunningham |first=Andrew |date=18 April 2023 |title=Intel unceremoniously dumps its year-old Blockscale chips for bitcoin mining |url=https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2023/04/intel-introduced-bitcoin-mining-chips-a-year-ago-and-theyre-already-going-away/ |access-date=19 April 2023 |website=Ars Technica |language=en-us |archive-date=19 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230419070248/https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2023/04/intel-introduced-bitcoin-mining-chips-a-year-ago-and-theyre-already-going-away/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Wallets===
[[File:A paper printable Bitcoin wallet consisting of one bitcoin address for receiving and the corresponding private key for spending.svg|thumb|An example paper printable Bitcoin wallet consisting of one Bitcoin address for receiving, and the corresponding private key for spending]]
{{Main|Cryptocurrency wallet}}

A [[cryptocurrency wallet]] is a means of storing the [[Public-key cryptography|public and private "keys"]] (address) or seed, which can be used to receive or spend the cryptocurrency.<ref>{{cite web|last=Arnott|first=Amy|date=2 August 2021|title=A Basic Glossary of Terms for Crypto Newbies|url=https://www.morningstar.com/articles/1050329/a-basic-glossary-of-terms-for-crypto-newbies|url-status=live|access-date=30 August 2021|website=Morningstar.com|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210802195320/https://www.morningstar.com/articles/1050329/a-basic-glossary-of-terms-for-crypto-newbies |archive-date=2 August 2021 }}</ref> With the private key, it is possible to write in the public ledger, effectively spending the associated cryptocurrency. With the public key, it is possible for others to send currency to the wallet.

There exist multiple methods of storing keys or seed in a wallet. These methods range from using paper wallets (which are public, private, or seed keys written on paper), to using hardware wallets (which are hardware to store your wallet information), to a digital wallet (which is a computer with software hosting your wallet information), to hosting your wallet using an exchange where cryptocurrency is traded, or by storing your wallet information on a digital medium such as plaintext.<ref>{{Cite journal|doi=10.5937/ekonomika1903065J|title=Comparative analysis of cryptocurrency wallets vs traditional wallets|year=2019|last1=Jokić|first1=Stevo|last2=Cvetković|first2=Aleksandar|last3=Adamović|first3=Saša|last4=Ristić|first4=Nenad|last5=Spalević|first5=Petar|journal=Ekonomika|volume=65|issue=3|pages=65–75|s2cid=208267171|doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Privacy===
{{Main|Blockchain privacy}}

Bitcoin is [[pseudonymous]], rather than [[Anonymous person|anonymous]]; the cryptocurrency in a wallet is not tied to a person but rather to one or more specific keys (or "addresses").<ref>{{Cite news |last=Lee |first=Justina |date=13 September 2018 |title=Mystery of the $2 Billion Bitcoin Whale That Fueled a Selloff |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-09-13/mystery-of-the-2-billion-bitcoin-whale-that-fueled-a-selloff |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181219093844/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-09-13/mystery-of-the-2-billion-bitcoin-whale-that-fueled-a-selloff |archive-date=19 December 2018 |newspaper=Bloomberg.com}}</ref> Thereby, bitcoin owners are not immediately identifiable, but all transactions are publicly available in the blockchain.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Galston |first1=Ezra |title=Untraceable Bitcoin Is a Myth |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/untraceable-bitcoin-is-a-myth-11623860828 |access-date=16 September 2022 |publisher=The Wall Street Journal |date=16 June 2021 |archive-date=20 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220920170550/https://www.wsj.com/articles/untraceable-bitcoin-is-a-myth-11623860828 |url-status=live }}</ref> Still, [[cryptocurrency exchanges]] are often required by law to collect the personal information of their users.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Goodell|first1=Geoff|last2=Aste|first2=Tomaso|date=2019|title=Can Cryptocurrencies Preserve Privacy and Comply With Regulations?|journal=Frontiers in Blockchain|volume=2|article-number=4|doi=10.3389/fbloc.2019.00004|issn=2624-7852|doi-access=free|arxiv=1811.12240}}</ref>

Some cryptocurrencies, such as [[Monero]], [[Zerocoin]], [[Zerocash]], and [[CryptoNote]], implement additional measures to increase privacy, such as by using [[zero-knowledge proofs]].<ref>{{cite web |title=What You Need To Know About Zero Knowledge |url=https://techcrunch.com/2015/02/07/what-you-need-to-know-about-zero-knowledge/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190220124117/https://techcrunch.com/2015/02/07/what-you-need-to-know-about-zero-knowledge/ |archive-date=20 February 2019 |access-date=19 December 2018 |website=TechCrunch|date=7 February 2015 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Greenberg |first=Andy |date=25 January 2017 |title=Monero, the Drug Dealer's Cryptocurrency of Choice, Is on Fire |magazine=Wired |url=https://www.wired.com/2017/01/monero-drug-dealers-cryptocurrency-choice-fire/ |url-status=live |access-date=19 December 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181210020727/https://www.wired.com/2017/01/monero-drug-dealers-cryptocurrency-choice-fire/ |archive-date=10 December 2018 |issn=1059-1028}}</ref>

A recent 2020 study presented different attacks on privacy in cryptocurrencies. The attacks demonstrated how the anonymity techniques are not sufficient safeguards. In order to improve privacy, researchers suggested several different ideas, including new cryptographic schemes and mechanisms for hiding the [[IP address]] of the source.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Herskind |first1=Lasse |last2=Katsikouli |first2=Panagiota |last3=Dragoni |first3=Nicola |date=2020 |title=Privacy and Cryptocurrencies—A Systematic Literature Review |journal=IEEE Access |volume=8 |pages=54044–54059 |doi=10.1109/ACCESS.2020.2980950 |issn=2169-3536|doi-access=free |bibcode=2020IEEEA...854044H }}</ref>

==Economics==
{{see also|Cryptoeconomics}}

Cryptocurrencies are used primarily outside banking and governmental institutions and are exchanged over the Internet.

===Block rewards===
Proof-of-work cryptocurrencies, such as bitcoin, offer block rewards incentives for miners. There has been an implicit belief that whether miners are paid by block rewards or transaction fees does not affect the security of the blockchain, but a study suggests that this may not be the case under certain circumstances.<ref>{{cite web |title=On the Instability of Bitcoin Without the Block Reward |url=https://www.cs.princeton.edu/~arvindn/publications/mining_CCS.pdf |access-date=5 May 2020 |archive-date=5 June 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200605042205/https://www.cs.princeton.edu/~arvindn/publications/mining_CCS.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

The rewards paid to miners increase the supply of the cryptocurrency. By making sure that verifying transactions is a costly business, the integrity of the network can be preserved as long as benevolent nodes control a majority of computing power. The verification algorithm requires a lot of processing power, and thus electricity, in order to make verification costly enough to accurately validate the public blockchain. Miners have to factor in the costs associated with expensive equipment necessary to stand a chance of solving a hash problem, and consider the significant amount of electrical power in search of the solution. Generally, the block rewards outweigh electricity and equipment costs, but this may not always be the case.<ref>{{cite web |title=Price Fluctuations and the Use of Bitcoin: An Empirical Inquiry |url=https://www.ecb.europa.eu/pub/conferences/shared/pdf/retpaym_150604/polasik_paper.pdf |access-date=5 May 2020 |archive-date=31 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201031161801/https://www.ecb.europa.eu/pub/conferences/shared/pdf/retpaym_150604/polasik_paper.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

The current value, not the long-term value, of the cryptocurrency supports the reward scheme to incentivize miners to engage in costly mining activities.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Yaish |first1=Aviv |last2=Zohar |first2=Aviv |date=18 June 2020 |title=Correct Cryptocurrency ASIC Pricing: Are Miners Overpaying? |series=Leibniz International Proceedings in Informatics (LIPIcs) |volume=282 |pages=2:1–2:25 |doi=10.4230/LIPIcs.AFT.2023.2 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2002.11064 |isbn=9783959773034 |s2cid=211296648 }}</ref> In 2018, bitcoin's design caused a 1.4% welfare loss compared to an efficient cash system, while a cash system with 2% money growth has a minor 0.003% welfare cost. The main source for this inefficiency is the large mining cost, which is estimated to be US$360 million per year. This translates into users being willing to accept a cash system with an inflation rate of 230% before being better off using bitcoin as a means of payment. However, the efficiency of the bitcoin system can be significantly improved by optimizing the rate of coin creation and minimizing transaction fees. Another potential improvement is to eliminate inefficient mining activities by changing the consensus protocol altogether.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Economics of Cryptocurrencies – Bitcoin and Beyond |url=https://www.bis.org/events/eopix_1810/chiu_paper.pdf |access-date=5 May 2020 |archive-date=10 December 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201210101527/https://www.bis.org/events/eopix_1810/chiu_paper.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Transaction fees===
Transaction fees (sometimes also referred to as ''miner fees'' or ''gas fees'') for cryptocurrency depend mainly on the [[supply and demand|supply]] of network capacity at the time, versus the [[supply and demand|demand]] from the currency holder for a faster transaction.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Electrum: Detailed Review and Full Guide On How To Use It |url=https://wallets.com/electrum-review/ |access-date=17 August 2024 |website=Wallets.com |language=en}}</ref> The ability for the holder to be allowed to set the fee manually often depends on the wallet software used, and central [[Cryptocurrency exchange|exchanges for cryptocurrency]] (CEX) usually do not allow the customer to set a custom transaction fee for the transaction.{{Citation needed|date=August 2024}} Their wallet software, such as [[Coinbase]] Wallet, however, might support adjusting the fee.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Coinbase Wallet > Adjusting network fees |url=https://help.coinbase.com/en/wallet/sending-and-receiving/adjusting-miner-fees#adjusting-your-transaction-speed |access-date=17 August 2024 |website=Coinbase Help}}</ref>

Select cryptocurrency exchanges have offered to let the user choose between different presets of transaction fee values during the currency conversion. One of those exchanges, namely '''LiteBit''', previously headquartered in the Netherlands, was forced to cease all operations in August 2023, "due to market changes and regulatory pressure".<ref>{{Cite web |title=LiteBit FAQ: Cease of operations |url=https://litebit.zendesk.com/hc/en-us/articles/8893147626268-FAQ-Cease-of-operations |access-date=17 August 2024 |website=LiteBit@Zendesk.com|date=22 May 2023 }}</ref>

The "recommended fee" suggested by the network will often depend on the time of day (due to depending on network load).

For [[Ethereum]], transaction fees differ by computational complexity, bandwidth use, and storage needs, while bitcoin transaction fees differ by transaction size and whether the transaction uses [[SegWit]]. In February 2023, the median transaction fee for Ether corresponded to $2.2845,<ref>{{cite web |title=Ethereum Median Transaction Fee historical chart |url=https://bitinfocharts.com/comparison/ethereum-median_transaction_fee.html#3m |url-status=live |access-date=19 March 2023 |website=BitInfoCharts |archive-date=14 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230414021933/https://bitinfocharts.com/comparison/ethereum-median_transaction_fee.html#3m }}</ref> while for bitcoin it corresponded to $0.659.<ref>{{cite web |title=Bitcoin Median Transaction Fee historical chart |url=https://bitinfocharts.com/comparison/bitcoin-median_transaction_fee.html#3m |url-status=live |access-date=19 March 2023 |archive-date=28 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230328075302/https://bitinfocharts.com/comparison/bitcoin-median_transaction_fee.html#3m }}</ref>

Some cryptocurrencies have no transaction fees, the most well-known example being [[Nano (cryptocurrency)|Nano (XNO)]], and instead rely on [[client-side]] proof-of-work as the transaction prioritization and anti-spam mechanism.<ref name="scalabilityOfBitcoinAndNano">{{Citation |title=Scalability of the Bitcoin and Nano protocols: a comparative analysis |date=2018 |url=http://www.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1229650/FULLTEXT02.pdf |publisher=Blekinge Institute of Technology |language=en-US |access-date=18 December 2019 |archive-date=19 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191219143645/http://www.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1229650/FULLTEXT02.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="comparativeAnalysis">{{Citation |last1=Pervez |first1=Huma |title=2018 12th International Conference on Open Source Systems and Technologies (ICOSST) |date=19 December 2018 |pages=27–34 |chapter=A Comparative Analysis of DAG-Based Blockchain Architectures |publisher=IEEE |language=en-US |doi=10.1109/ICOSST.2018.8632193 |isbn=978-1-5386-9564-7 |last2=Muneeb |first2=Muhammad |last3=Irfan |first3=Muhammad Usama |last4=Haq |first4=Irfan Ul |s2cid=59601449}}</ref><ref name="blockchainCompared">{{Citation |last1=Bencic |first1=Federico Matteo |title=2018 IEEE 38th International Conference on Distributed Computing Systems (ICDCS) |date=26 April 2018 |pages=1569–1570 |chapter=Distributed Ledger Technology: Blockchain Compared to Directed Acyclic Graph |publisher=University of Zagreb |language=en-US |arxiv=1804.10013 |doi=10.1109/ICDCS.2018.00171 |isbn=978-1-5386-6871-9 |last2=Podnar Zarko |first2=Ivana |s2cid=13741873}}</ref>

===Exchanges===
{{Main|Cryptocurrency exchange}}

[[Cryptocurrency exchange]]s allow customers to trade cryptocurrencies<ref>{{Cite web |date=2 November 2021 |title=Banks Should Be Allowed to Trade Crypto {{!}} by cxihub {{!}} Nov 2021 {{!}} The Open Finance Journal |url=https://news.cxihub.com/banks-should-be-allowed-to-trade-crypto-aaee5a23c5ad?gi=bb64c7b5062f |access-date=17 August 2022 |archive-date=2 November 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211102044952/https://news.cxihub.com/banks-should-be-allowed-to-trade-crypto-aaee5a23c5ad?gi=bb64c7b5062f |url-status=dead }}</ref> for other assets, such as conventional [[fiat money]], or to trade between different digital currencies.

Crypto marketplaces do not guarantee that an investor is completing a purchase or trade at the optimal price. As a result, as of 2020, it was possible to [[arbitrage]] to find the difference in price across several markets.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Makarov |first1=Igor |last2=Schoar |first2=Antoinette |date=2020 |title=Trading and arbitrage in cryptocurrency markets |journal=Journal of Financial Economics |language=en |volume=135 |issue=2 |pages=293–319 |doi=10.1016/j.jfineco.2019.07.001 |s2cid=53072748 |url=https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/100409/ |access-date=7 February 2023 |archive-date=8 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230208233921/https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/100409/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Atomic swaps===
Atomic swaps are a mechanism where one cryptocurrency can be exchanged directly for another cryptocurrency without the need for a trusted third party, such as an exchange.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Xu |first1=Jiahua |last2=Ackerer |first2=Damien |last3=Dubovitskaya |first3=Alevtina |title=2021 IEEE 41st International Conference on Distributed Computing Systems (ICDCS) |chapter=A Game-Theoretic Analysis of Cross-Chain Atomic Swaps with HTLCS |pages=584–594 |doi=10.1109/ICDCS51616.2021.00062 |date=July 2021 |arxiv=2011.11325 |isbn=978-1-6654-4513-9 |s2cid=227126965 }}</ref>

===ATMs===
[[File:Bitcoin Teller SIBOS Boston 2014 2.jpg|upright|thumb|A [[Bitcoin ATM]]]]

Jordan Kelley, founder of [[Bitcoin ATM|Robocoin]], launched the first [[bitcoin ATM]] in the United States in February 2014. The kiosk installed in Austin, Texas, is similar to bank ATMs but has scanners to read government-issued identification such as a driver's license, or a passport to confirm users' identities.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Wahba |first=Phil |date=18 February 2014 |title=First U.S. bitcoin ATMs to open soon in Seattle, Austin |language=en |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-bitcoin-robocoin-idUSBREA1H05F20140218 |url-status=live |access-date=17 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151019092802/http://www.reuters.com/article/2014/02/18/us-bitcoin-robocoin-idUSBREA1H05F20140218 |archive-date=19 October 2015}}</ref>

===Initial coin offerings===
An [[initial coin offering]] (ICO) is a controversial means of raising funds for a new cryptocurrency venture. An ICO may be used by startups with the intention of avoiding regulation. However, securities regulators in many jurisdictions, including in the U.S. and Canada, have indicated that if a coin or token is an "investment contract" (e.g., under the Howey test, i.e., an investment of money with a reasonable expectation of profit based significantly on the entrepreneurial or managerial efforts of others), it is a security and is subject to securities regulation. In an ICO campaign, a percentage of the cryptocurrency (usually in the form of "tokens") is sold to early backers of the project in exchange for legal tender or other cryptocurrencies, often bitcoin or Ether.<ref>{{cite web |date=24 August 2017 |title=CSA Staff Notice 46-307 Cryptocurrency Offerings |url=http://www.osc.gov.on.ca/en/SecuritiesLaw_csa_20170824_cryptocurrency-offerings.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170929101456/http://www.osc.gov.on.ca/en/SecuritiesLaw_csa_20170824_cryptocurrency-offerings.htm |archive-date=29 September 2017 |access-date=20 January 2018 |website=Ontario Securities Commission}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=25 July 2017 |title=SEC Issues Investigative Report Concluding DAO Tokens, a Digital Asset, Were Securities |url=https://www.sec.gov/news/press-release/2017-131 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171010022343/https://www.sec.gov/news/press-release/2017-131 |archive-date=10 October 2017 |access-date=20 January 2018 |website=sec.gov}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=11 December 2017 |title=Company Halts ICO After SEC Raises Registration Concerns |url=https://www.sec.gov/news/press-release/2017-227 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180119192823/https://www.sec.gov/news/press-release/2017-227 |archive-date=19 January 2018 |access-date=20 January 2018 |website=sec.gov}}</ref>

According to [[PricewaterhouseCoopers]], four of the 10 biggest proposed initial coin offerings have used [[Switzerland]] as a base, where they are frequently registered as non-profit foundations. The Swiss regulatory agency [[Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority|FINMA]] stated that it would take a "balanced approach" to ICO projects and would allow "legitimate innovators to navigate the regulatory landscape and so launch their projects in a way consistent with national laws protecting investors and the integrity of the financial system." In response to numerous requests by industry representatives, a legislative ICO working group began to issue legal guidelines in 2018, which are intended to remove uncertainty from cryptocurrency offerings and to establish sustainable business practices.<ref>{{Cite news |date=16 February 2018 |title=Switzerland sets out guidelines to support initial coin offerings |work=Financial Times |url=https://www.ft.com/content/52820f90-1307-11e8-940e-08320fc2a277 |url-status=live |access-date=17 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180527201759/https://www.ft.com/content/52820f90-1307-11e8-940e-08320fc2a277 |archive-date=27 May 2018}}</ref>

===Price trends===
The [[market capitalization]] of a cryptocurrency is calculated by multiplying the price by the number of coins in circulation. The total cryptocurrency market cap has historically been dominated by bitcoin accounting for at least 50% of the market cap value where altcoins have increased and decreased in market cap value in relation to bitcoin. Bitcoin's value is largely determined by speculation among other technological limiting factors known as blockchain rewards coded into the architecture technology of bitcoin itself.<ref name="auto">{{cite journal |last1=Meynkhard |first1=Artur |title=Fair market value of bitcoin: halving effect |journal=Investment Management and Financial Innovations |date=28 November 2019 |volume=16 |issue=4 |pages=72–85 |doi=10.21511/imfi.16(4).2019.07 |s2cid=212850773 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

The cryptocurrency market cap follows a trend known as the "halving", which is when the block rewards received from bitcoin are halved due to technological mandated limited factors instilled into bitcoin which in turn limits the supply of bitcoin. As the date reaches near of a halving (twice thus far historically) the cryptocurrency market cap increases, followed by a downtrend.<ref name="auto"/>

By June 2021, cryptocurrency had begun to be offered by some wealth managers in the US for [[401(k)]]s.<ref>{{cite web |last=Harris |first=Craig |date=10 June 2021 |title=Cryptocurrency to become option for some workers' 401(k) retirement plans, WSJ reports |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/2021/06/10/bitcoin-investing-cryptocurrency-401-k-retirement-plans-launched/7640161002/ |website=USA TODAY |access-date=16 June 2021 |archive-date=14 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210614041617/https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/2021/06/10/bitcoin-investing-cryptocurrency-401-k-retirement-plans-launched/7640161002/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Morris |first=Chris |date=10 June 2021 |title=Coinbase will let you add crypto to your 401(k) through new deal |url=https://fortune.com/2021/06/10/coinbase-crypto-401k-roth-offering-forusall/ |website=Fortune |access-date=16 June 2021 |archive-date=20 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210620021241/https://fortune.com/2021/06/10/coinbase-crypto-401k-roth-offering-forusall/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Asymkos |first=Stephanie |date=10 June 2021 |title=Bitcoin and crypto go mainstream with new 401(k) retirement offering |url=https://money.yahoo.com/bitcoin-crypto-investing-goes-mainstream-in-new-401-k-offering-214411478.html |website=money.yahoo.com |access-date=16 June 2021 |archive-date=17 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210617162820/https://money.yahoo.com/bitcoin-crypto-investing-goes-mainstream-in-new-401-k-offering-214411478.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Volatility===
Cryptocurrency prices are much more volatile than established financial assets such as [[stock]]s. For example, over one week in May 2022, bitcoin lost 20% of its value and Ethereum lost 26%, while [[Solana (blockchain platform)|Solana]] and [[Cardano (blockchain platform)|Cardano]] lost 41% and 35% respectively. The falls were attributed to warnings about inflation. By comparison, in the same week, the [[Nasdaq-100|Nasdaq]] tech stock index fell 7.6 per cent and the [[FTSE 100 Index|FTSE 100]] was 3.6 per cent down.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Russell-Jones |first=Lily |date=15 May 2022 |title=What's happening to cryptocurrencies? |work=Sunday Times |url-access=subscription |url=https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/markets/article/whats-happening-to-cryptocurrencies-hdlklltrk |archive-date=22 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220522225818/https://www.thetimes.co.uk/article/whats-happening-to-cryptocurrencies-hdlklltrk |url-status=live |access-date=1 June 2022 }}</ref>

In the longer term, of the [[List of cryptocurrencies|10 leading cryptocurrencies]] identified by the total value of coins in circulation in January 2018, only four (bitcoin, Ethereum, Cardano and [[Ripple (payment protocol)|Ripple]] (XRP)) were still in that position in early 2022.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Tetrina |first=Kat |date=1 March 2022 |title=Top 10 Cryptocurrencies In March 2022 |work=Forbes |url=https://www.forbes.com/advisor/investing/top-10-cryptocurrencies/ |access-date=1 June 2022 |archive-date=5 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220405164804/https://www.forbes.com/advisor/investing/top-10-cryptocurrencies/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The total value of all cryptocurrencies was  $2 trillion at the end of 2021, but had halved nine months later.<ref>{{Cite news |date=30 November 2021 |title=A history of cryptocurrency, from gaming tokens to a $2tn market |work=Financial Times |url=https://www.ft.com/content/78431430-1afb-4712-bb75-424788c60583 |access-date=24 October 2022 |archive-date=24 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221024133432/https://www.ft.com/content/78431430-1afb-4712-bb75-424788c60583 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Russell-Jones |first=Lily |date=7 September 2022 |title=Cryptocurrency market slumps below $1trn |newspaper=[[The Times]] |issn=0140-0460 |language=en |url-access=subscription |url=https://www.thetimes.com/article/cryptocurrency-market-slumps-below-1trn-q0rb8ls9v |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220925203033/https://www.thetimes.co.uk/article/cryptocurrency-market-slumps-below-1trn-q0rb8ls9v |archive-date=25 September 2022 |url-status=live |access-date=24 October 2022 }}</ref> The ''Wall Street Journal'' has commented that the crypto sector has become "intertwined" with the rest of the capital markets and "sensitive to the same forces that drive tech stocks and other risk assets," such as inflation forecasts.<ref>{{Cite news |title=Bitcoin, Other Cryptos Fall on Hot Inflation Report |url=https://www.wsj.com/livecoverage/stock-market-news-today-09-13-2022/card/bitcoin-and-other-cryptos-fall-on-hot-inflation-report-wC8EiM4cyizUxCZcsBzz |access-date=24 October 2022 |website=WSJ |language=en |archive-date=24 October 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221024133432/https://www.wsj.com/livecoverage/stock-market-news-today-09-13-2022/card/bitcoin-and-other-cryptos-fall-on-hot-inflation-report-wC8EiM4cyizUxCZcsBzz |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Databases===
There are also ''centralized'' databases, outside of blockchains, that store crypto market data. Compared to the blockchain, databases perform fast as there is no verification process. Four of the most popular cryptocurrency market databases are [[CoinMarketCap]], CoinGecko, BraveNewCoin, and Cryptocompare.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Vidal-Tomás |first=David |date=2022 |title=Which cryptocurrency data sources should scholars use? |journal=International Review of Financial Analysis |volume=81 |article-number=102061 |doi=10.1016/j.irfa.2022.102061 }}</ref>

==Social and political aspects==
{{See also|Crypto-anarchism|Cypherpunk}}

According to Alan Feuer of ''[[The New York Times]]'', [[libertarian]]s and [[anarcho-capitalist]]s were attracted to the philosophical idea behind bitcoin. Early bitcoin supporter [[Roger Ver]] said: "At first, almost everyone who got involved did so for philosophical reasons. We saw bitcoin as a great idea, as a way to separate money from the state."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Feuer |first=Alan |date=14 December 2013 |title=The Bitcoin Ideology |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/12/15/sunday-review/the-bitcoin-ideology.html |access-date=1 March 2022 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=1 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180701222302/https://www.nytimes.com/2013/12/15/sunday-review/the-bitcoin-ideology.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Economist [[Paul Krugman]] argues that cryptocurrencies like bitcoin are "something of a cult" based in "paranoid fantasies" of government power.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Krugman |first=Paul |date=29 January 2018 |title=Opinion {{!}} Bubble, Bubble, Fraud and Trouble |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/01/29/opinion/bitcoin-bubble-fraud.html |access-date=1 March 2022 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=4 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180604124251/https://www.nytimes.com/2018/01/29/opinion/bitcoin-bubble-fraud.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[David Golumbia]] says that the ideas influencing bitcoin advocates emerge from right-wing extremist movements such as the [[Liberty Lobby]] and the [[John Birch Society]] and their anti-Central Bank rhetoric, or, more recently, [[Ron Paul]] and [[Tea Party movement|Tea Party]]-style libertarianism.<ref>{{cite web |date=28 October 2016 |title=Review of "The Politics of Bitcoin: Software as Right-Wing Extremism" |url=https://www.newsclick.in/review-politics-bitcoin-software-right-wing-extremism |access-date=1 March 2022 |website=NewsClick |language=en |archive-date=1 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220301164202/https://www.newsclick.in/review-politics-bitcoin-software-right-wing-extremism |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Steve Bannon]], who owns a "good stake" in bitcoin, sees cryptocurrency as a form of disruptive populism, taking control back from central authorities.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Peters |first1=Jeremy W. |last2=Popper |first2=Nathaniel |date=14 June 2018 |title=Stephen Bannon Buys Into Bitcoin |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/06/14/technology/steve-bannon-bitcoin.html |access-date=1 March 2022 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=1 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180701015803/https://www.nytimes.com/2018/06/14/technology/steve-bannon-bitcoin.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Bitcoin's founder, [[Satoshi Nakamoto]], supported the idea that cryptocurrencies go well with libertarianism. "It's very attractive to the libertarian viewpoint if we can explain it properly," Nakamoto said in 2008.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bitcoin P2P e-cash paper {{!}} Satoshi Nakamoto Institute |url=https://satoshi.nakamotoinstitute.org/emails/cryptography/12/ |access-date=10 March 2022 |website=satoshi.nakamotoinstitute.org |date=14 November 2008 |archive-date=1 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220301185407/https://satoshi.nakamotoinstitute.org/emails/cryptography/12/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

According to the [[European Central Bank]], the decentralization of money offered by bitcoin has its theoretical roots in the [[Austrian school of economics]], especially with [[Friedrich von Hayek]] in his book [[The Denationalisation of Money|''Denationalisation of Money: The Argument Refined'']],<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hayek |first=Friedrich A. von (Friedrich August) |url=http://archive.org/details/denationalisatio0000haye |title=Denationalisation of money : the argument refined; an analysis of the theory and practice of concurrent currencies |date=1990 |publisher=London : Institute of Economic Affairs |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-255-36239-9}}</ref> in which Hayek advocates a complete [[free market]] in the production, distribution and management of money to end the monopoly of [[central banks]].<ref>{{citation |url=https://www.ecb.europa.eu/pub/pdf/other/virtualcurrencyschemes201210en.pdf |title=Virtual Currency Schemes |date=October 2012 |publisher=European Central Bank |isbn=978-92-899-0862-7 |access-date=1 March 2022 |archive-date=25 May 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180525031305/http://www.ecb.europa.eu/pub/pdf/other/virtualcurrencyschemes201210en.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Baldwin |first1=Jon |title=In digital we trust: Bitcoin discourse, digital currencies, and decentralized network fetishism |journal=[[Palgrave Communications]] |date=2018 |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=1–10 |article-number=14 |doi=10.1057/s41599-018-0065-0 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Usage==
===International transfers===
Monthly cryptocurrency transfers under $10,000 to and from Africa reached $316 million in June 2020, according to Chainalysis data. Reuters reported that bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies are unregulated in many countries and their legal status is unclear, meaning there is no safety net and little recourse for lost funds.<ref>{{Cite news |title=How bitcoin met the real world in Africa |work=Reuters |date=2020-09-08 |url=https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/how-bitcoin-met-real-world-africa-2020-09-08/ |access-date=2026-03-02}}</ref>

Some migrants in the United Arab Emirates used cryptocurrencies to send [[remittances]] home, claiming lower fees compared with traditional remittance services.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Farouk |first=Menna |title=FEATURE-Migrants in UAE turn to crypto to send remittances home |work=Thomson Reuters Foundation |publisher=Reuters |date=2023-06-09 |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/world/feature-migrants-in-uae-turn-to-crypto-to-send-remittances-home-idUSL8N37R1Z2/ |access-date=2026-03-02}}</ref>

=== Institutional balance-sheet holdings ===
In 2025, some publicly traded companies announced plans to raise capital to buy and hold bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies as treasury assets.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Zuckerman |first=Gregory |last2=Huang |first2=Vicky Ge |title=The Hottest Business Strategy This Summer Is Buying Crypto |work=The Wall Street Journal |url=https://www.livemint.com/companies/news/the-hottest-business-strategy-this-summer-is-buying-crypto-11753494891312.html |via=LiveMint |date=2025-07-25 |access-date=2026-02-27}}</ref> Reuters reported that the inherent volatility of crypto tokens makes them a poor fit for boards with a low risk appetite, potentially limiting their appeal beyond core industry players.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Nishant |first=Niket |last2=Saini |first2=Manya |date=2025-08-05 |title=Small public companies snap up ether in new crypto gold rush, even as risks linger |url=https://www.reuters.com/business/small-public-companies-snap-up-ether-new-crypto-gold-rush-even-risks-linger-2025-08-05/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250809022341/https://www.reuters.com/business/small-public-companies-snap-up-ether-new-crypto-gold-rush-even-risks-linger-2025-08-05/ |archive-date=2025-08-09 |access-date=2026-02-27 |work=Reuters |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Regulation==
{{Main|Regulation of cryptocurrency}}

The rise in the popularity of cryptocurrencies and their adoption by financial institutions has led some governments to assess whether regulation is needed to protect users.
