The [[Financial Action Task Force]] (FATF) has defined cryptocurrency-related services as "virtual asset service providers" (VASPs) and recommended that they be regulated with the same [[money laundering]] ([[Money laundering#Combating|AML]]) and [[know your customer]] (KYC) requirements as financial institutions.<ref>{{citation |publisher=FATF |date=2019 |title=Guidance for a Risk-Based Approach to Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers |url=https://www.fatf-gafi.org/publications/fatfrecommendations/documents/guidance-rba-virtual-assets.html |access-date=22 July 2021 |archive-date=26 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210726121248/https://www.fatf-gafi.org/publications/fatfrecommendations/documents/guidance-rba-virtual-assets.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

In May 2020, the Joint Working Group on interVASP Messaging Standards published "IVMS 101", a universal common language for communication of required originator and beneficiary information between VASPs. The FATF and financial regulators were informed as the data model was developed.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://intervasp.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/IVMS101-interVASP-data-model-standard-issue-1-FINAL.pdf | title=interVASP Messaging Standards | website=intervasp.org | access-date=13 October 2021 | archive-date=9 October 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211009220925/https://intervasp.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/05/IVMS101-interVASP-data-model-standard-issue-1-FINAL.pdf | url-status=live }}</ref>

In June 2020, FATF updated its guidance to include the "Travel Rule" for cryptocurrencies, a measure which mandates that VASPs obtain, hold, and exchange information about the originators and beneficiaries of virtual asset transfers.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.fatf-gafi.org/media/fatf/documents/recommendations/12-Month-Review-Revised-FATF-Standards-Virtual-Assets-VASPS.pdf |title=12-Month Review of the Revised FATF Standards on Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers |website=www.fatf-gafi.org |access-date=13 October 2021 |language=en |archive-date=28 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211028171409/https://www.fatf-gafi.org/media/fatf/documents/recommendations/12-Month-Review-Revised-FATF-Standards-Virtual-Assets-VASPS.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> Subsequent standardized protocol specifications recommended using [[JSON]] for relaying data between VASPs and identity services. As of December 2020, the IVMS 101 data model has yet to be finalized and ratified by the three global standard setting bodies that created it.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://tsc.bitcoinassociation.net/standards/travel-rule-specification/ | title=Travel Rule Specification - Bitcoin SV Technical Standards | website=tsc.bitcoinassociation.net | access-date=13 October 2021 | archive-date=27 October 2021 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211027183645/https://tsc.bitcoinassociation.net/standards/travel-rule-specification/ | url-status=live }}</ref>

The European Commission published a digital finance strategy in September 2020. This included a draft regulation on Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA), which aimed to provide a comprehensive regulatory framework for digital assets in the EU.<ref>{{citation |publisher=European Commission |title=Proposal for regulation of Markets in Crypto-assets, and amending Directive (EU) 2019/1937 |date=24 September 2020 |url=https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:52020PC0593&from=EN |access-date=23 August 2021 |archive-date=23 August 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210823212123/https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:52020PC0593&from=EN |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{citation |first1=Dirk A. |last1=Zetzsche |first2=Filippo |last2=Annunziata |first3=Douglas W. |last3=Arner |first4=Kerry |last4=Holdings |first5=Ross P. |last5=Buckley |title=The Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) and the EU Digital Finance Strategy |date=30 November 2020 |url=https://www.law.ox.ac.uk/business-law-blog/blog/2020/11/markets-crypto-assets-regulation-mica-and-eu-digital-finance-strategy |publisher=University of Oxford Faculty of Law |access-date=23 August 2021 |archive-date=23 August 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210823212133/https://www.law.ox.ac.uk/business-law-blog/blog/2020/11/markets-crypto-assets-regulation-mica-and-eu-digital-finance-strategy |url-status=live }}</ref>

In June 2021, the [[Basel Committee on Banking Supervision]] proposed that banks that held cryptocurrency assets must set aside capital to cover all potential losses. For instance, if a bank were to hold bitcoin worth $2 billion, it would be required to set aside enough capital to cover the entire $2 billion. This is a more extreme standard than banks are usually held to when it comes to other assets. However, this is a proposal and not a regulation.

The IMF has sought seeking a coordinated, consistent and comprehensive approach to supervising cryptocurrencies. [[Tobias Adrian]], the IMF's financial counsellor and head of its monetary and capital markets department said in a January 2022 interview that "Agreeing global regulations is never quick. But if we start now, we can achieve the goal of maintaining financial stability while also enjoying the benefits which the underlying technological innovations bring,"<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.ft.com/content/45ca2229-485e-4043-b709-deda943e9ddb|title=Crypto risks 'destabilising' emerging markets, says senior IMF official|first=Chris|last=Flood|newspaper=Financial Times|date=31 January 2022|access-date=31 January 2022|archive-date=31 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220131120346/https://www.ft.com/content/45ca2229-485e-4043-b709-deda943e9ddb|url-status=live}}</ref>

In May 2024, 15 years after the advent of the first blockchain, bitcoin, the [[US Congress]] advanced a bill to the full [[United States House of Representatives|House of Representatives]] to provide regulatory clarity for digital assets. The [[Financial Innovation and Technology for the 21st Century Act]], which defines responsibilities between various US agencies, notably between the [[Commodity Futures Trading Commission]] (CFTC) for decentralized blockchains and the [[Securities and Exchange Commission]] (SEC) for blockchains that are functional but not decentralized.  [[Stablecoin]]s are excluded from both CFTC and SEC regulation in this bill, "except for fraud and certain activities by registered firms."<ref name=cfins20240510>{{cite news |title=House Digital Asset Legislation, the Financial Innovation and Technology for the 21st Century Act, Takes Another Step Forward |url=https://www.crowdfundinsider.com/2024/05/224888-house-digital-asset-legislation-the-financial-innovation-and-technology-for-the-21st-century-act-takes-another-step-forward/ |last=Alois |first=JD |work=Crowdfund Insider |date=10 May 2024 |access-date=14 May 2024 |archive-date=13 May 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240513211635/https://www.crowdfundinsider.com/2024/05/224888-house-digital-asset-legislation-the-financial-innovation-and-technology-for-the-21st-century-act-takes-another-step-forward/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

===China===
In September 2017, China banned [[Initial coin offering|ICOs]] to cause [[abnormal return]] from cryptocurrency decreasing during announcement window. The liquidity changes by banning ICOs in China was temporarily negative while the liquidity effect became positive after news.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Sijia |last2=Gregoriou |first2=Andros |date=27 November 2020 |title=The price and liquidity impact of China forbidding initial coin offerings on the cryptocurrency market |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13504851.2020.1713979 |journal=Applied Economics Letters |language=en |volume=27 |issue=20 |pages=1695–1698 |doi=10.1080/13504851.2020.1713979 |s2cid=214099348 |issn=1350-4851 |access-date=4 August 2022 |archive-date=4 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220804220846/https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/13504851.2020.1713979 |url-status=live }}</ref>

On 18 May 2021, China banned financial institutions and payment companies from being able to provide cryptocurrency transaction related services.<ref>{{cite web|date=18 May 2021|title=China bans financial, payment institutions from cryptocurrency business|url=https://www.reuters.com/technology/chinese-financial-payment-bodies-barred-cryptocurrency-business-2021-05-18/|access-date=12 July 2021|website=Reuters|archive-date=11 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210711224318/https://www.reuters.com/technology/chinese-financial-payment-bodies-barred-cryptocurrency-business-2021-05-18/|url-status=live}}</ref> This led to a sharp fall in the price of the biggest [[proof of work]] cryptocurrencies. For instance, [[bitcoin]] fell 31%, [[Ethereum]] fell 44%, [[Binance#BNB|Binance Coin]] fell 32% and [[Dogecoin]] fell 30%.<ref>{{cite web |first=Shalini |last=Nagarajan |title=Bitcoin tumbles as low as $30,000 amid a broad crypto sell-off after China signals a crackdown |work=Business Insider |date=19 May 2021 |url=https://markets.businessinsider.com/currencies/news/bitcoin-price-cryptocurrencies-china-crypto-crackdown-price-outlook-2021-5 |access-date=12 July 2021 |archive-date=12 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210712192106/https://markets.businessinsider.com/currencies/news/bitcoin-price-cryptocurrencies-china-crypto-crackdown-price-outlook-2021-5 |url-status=live }}</ref> Proof of work mining was the next focus, with regulators in popular mining regions citing the use of electricity generated from highly polluting sources such as coal to create bitcoin and Ethereum.<ref>{{cite web |first1=Samuel |last1=Shen |first2=Alun |last2=John |date=19 June 2021 |title=China's cryptocurrency-mining crackdown spreads to Sichuan |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/technology/chinas-cryptocurrency-mining-crackdown-spreads-sichuan-2021-06-19/ |access-date=9 May 2022 |archive-date=20 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220520161521/https://www.reuters.com/technology/chinas-cryptocurrency-mining-crackdown-spreads-sichuan-2021-06-19/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In September 2021, the Chinese government outlawed all cryptocurrency transactions, completing its crackdown on cryptocurrency.<ref name="BBC News"/>

===Cook Islands===
In April 2024, [[TVNZ]]'s [[1News]] reported that the [[Cook Islands]] government was proposing legislation that would allow "recovery agents" to use various means including hacking to investigate or find cryptocurrency that may have been used for illegal means or is the "proceeds of crime." The Tainted Cryptocurrency Recovery Bill was drafted by two lawyers hired by US-based debt collection company Drumcliffe. The proposed legislation was criticised by Cook Islands Crown Law's deputy solicitor general David Greig, who described it as "flawed" and said that some provisions were "clearly unconstitutional". The Cook Islands Financial Services Development Authority described Drumcliffe's involvement as a conflict of interest.<ref name="1 News Cook Islands">{{cite news |last1=Dreaver |first1=Barbara |title='Spy film type thing' - Alarm grows over Cook Islands cryptocurrency bill |url=https://www.1news.co.nz/2024/04/14/spy-film-type-thing-alarm-grows-over-cook-islands-cryptocurrency-bill/ |access-date=18 April 2024 |work=[[1News]] |publisher=[[TVNZ]] |date=14 April 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240418105529/https://www.1news.co.nz/2024/04/14/spy-film-type-thing-alarm-grows-over-cook-islands-cryptocurrency-bill/ |archive-date=18 April 2024}}</ref>

Similar criticism was echoed by [[Auckland University of Technology]] cryptocurrency specialist and senior lecturer Jeff Nijsse and [[University of Otago]] [[Political science|political scientist]] Professor [[Robert Patman]], who described it as government overreach and described it as inconsistent with international law. Since the Cook Islands is an [[associated state]] that is part of the [[Realm of New Zealand]], Patman said that the law would have "implications for New Zealand's governance arrangements." A spokesperson for [[Minister of Foreign Affairs (New Zealand)|New Zealand Foreign Minister]] [[Winston Peters]] confirmed that New Zealand officials were discussing the legislation with their Cook Islands counterparts.  [[Prime Minister of the Cook Islands|Cook Islands Prime Minister]] [[Mark Brown (Cook Islands)|Mark Brown]] defended the legislation as part of the territory's fight against international cybercrime.<ref name="1 News Cook Islands" />

===El Salvador===
{{Update|part=section|date=November 2025|reason=}}

On 9 June 2021, [[El Salvador]] announced that it will adopt [[bitcoin]] as legal tender, becoming the first country to do so.<ref name="reuters.com">{{cite web|date=9 June 2021|title=In a world first, El Salvador makes bitcoin legal tender|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/el-salvador-approves-first-law-bitcoin-legal-tender-2021-06-09/|access-date=14 July 2021|website=Reuters|archive-date=12 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210812023227/https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/el-salvador-approves-first-law-bitcoin-legal-tender-2021-06-09/|url-status=live}}</ref>

===EU===
{{main|Markets in Crypto-Assets}}

The EU defines crypto assets as "a digital representation of a value or of a right that is able to be transferred and stored electronically using distributed ledger technology or similar technology."<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://finance.ec.europa.eu/digital-finance/crypto-assets_en|title=Crypto-assets - European Commission|website=finance.ec.europa.eu}}</ref> The EU regulation Markets in Crypto-Assets (MiCA) covering asset-referenced tokens (ARTs) and electronic money tokens (EMTs) (also known as stablecoins) came into force on 30 June 2024. As of 17 January 2025, the [[European Securities and Markets Authority]] (ESMA) issued guidance to crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) allowing them to maintain crypto-asset services for non-compliant ARTs and EMTs until the end of March 2025.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.esma.europa.eu/publications-data/questions-answers/2404|title=ESMA_QA_2404|website=www.esma.europa.eu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.williamfry.com/knowledge/esma-statement-on-services-re-non-micar-compliant-art-emts/|title=ESMA Statement On services Re Non-MiCAR-Compliant ART/EMTs|first=Ashley|last=Hennessy|date=27 January 2025|website=WILLIAM FRY}}</ref>

The rest of MiCA came into force as of 30 December 2024, covering crypto-assets other than ART and EMT and CASPs. MiCA excludes crypto-assets if they qualify as financial instruments according to ESMA guidelines published on 17 December 2024 as well as crypto-assets that are unique and not fungible with other crypto-assets.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dlapiper.com/en/insights/publications/2025/01/articleeu-crypto-assets-regulatory-framework|title=EU crypto-assets regulatory framework: application of the landmark Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA)|website=DLA Piper}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.klgates.com/The-Regulation-on-Markets-in-Crypto-Assets-Becomes-Fully-Applicable-in-All-Member-States-of-the-European-Union-1-24-2025|title=The Regulation on Markets in Crypto-Assets Becomes Fully Applicable in All Member States of the European Union|website=www.klgates.com}}</ref>

===India===
At present, India neither prohibits nor allows investment in the cryptocurrency market. In 2020, the Supreme Court of India had lifted the ban on cryptocurrency, which was imposed by the Reserve Bank of India.<ref>{{cite web|date=18 September 2021|title=RBI Lost Case on Cryptocurrency in Supreme Court, It Must Stop Behaving Like Sore Loser|url=https://www.news18.com/news/opinion/rbi-lost-case-on-cryptocurrency-in-supreme-court-it-must-stop-behaving-like-sore-loser-4196594.html|access-date=24 January 2022|website=News18|archive-date=24 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220124051652/https://www.news18.com/news/opinion/rbi-lost-case-on-cryptocurrency-in-supreme-court-it-must-stop-behaving-like-sore-loser-4196594.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Perumal|first=Prashanth|date=2 June 2021|title=Future of cryptocurrency in India continues to hang in the balance|language=en-IN|work=The Hindu|url=https://www.thehindu.com/business/future-of-cryptocurrency-in-india-continues-to-hang-in-the-balance/article34704676.ece|access-date=24 January 2022|issn=0971-751X|archive-date=24 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220124053149/https://www.thehindu.com/business/future-of-cryptocurrency-in-india-continues-to-hang-in-the-balance/article34704676.ece|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date=1 December 2021|title=From ban to regulation, cryptocurrency's journey so far in India|url=https://indianexpress.com/article/technology/crypto/cryptocurrency-in-india-a-look-at-the-regulatory-journey-of-cryptocurrencies-7648767/|access-date=24 January 2022|website=The Indian Express|archive-date=24 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220124051648/https://indianexpress.com/article/technology/crypto/cryptocurrency-in-india-a-look-at-the-regulatory-journey-of-cryptocurrencies-7648767/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=SC Verdict On Cryptocurrencies: What It Means For Investors|url=https://www.moneycontrol.com/news/business/personal-finance/sc-verdict-on-cryptocurrencies-what-it-means-for-investors-5070381.html|access-date=24 January 2022|website=Moneycontrol|date=25 March 2020|archive-date=24 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220124051654/https://www.moneycontrol.com/news/business/personal-finance/sc-verdict-on-cryptocurrencies-what-it-means-for-investors-5070381.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Since then, an investment in cryptocurrency is considered legitimate, though there is still ambiguity about the issues regarding the extent and payment of tax on the income accrued thereupon and also its regulatory regime. But it is being contemplated that the Indian Parliament will soon pass a specific law to either ban or regulate the cryptocurrency market in India.<ref>{{cite web|work=Deutsche Welle|title=Why is the Indian government cracking down on cryptocurrency?|url=https://www.dw.com/en/why-is-the-indian-government-cracking-down-on-cryptocurrency/a-60148889|access-date=24 January 2022|archive-date=28 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220128213818/https://www.dw.com/en/why-is-the-indian-government-cracking-down-on-cryptocurrency/a-60148889|url-status=live}}</ref>

Expressing his public policy opinion on the Indian cryptocurrency market to a well-known online publication, a leading [[public policy]] lawyer and Vice President of [[South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation|SAARCLAW]] (South Asian Association for Regional Co-operation in Law) [[Hemant Batra]] has said that the "cryptocurrency market has now become very big with involvement of billions of dollars in the market hence, it is now unattainable and irreconcilable for the government to completely ban all sorts of cryptocurrency and its trading and investment".<ref>{{cite web |author=Shashwat Mishra |date=15 January 2022 |title=The Crypto Effect : Framework, challenges & The way forward |url=https://www.mumbaiuncensored.com/2022/01/15/the-crypto-effect-framework-challenges-the-way-forward/  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220124050010/https://www.mumbaiuncensored.com/2022/01/15/the-crypto-effect-framework-challenges-the-way-forward/ |archive-date=24 January 2022 |url-status=usurped |access-date=24 January 2022 }}</ref> He mooted regulating the cryptocurrency market rather than completely banning it. He favoured following [[International Monetary Fund|IMF]] and [[Financial Action Task Force|FATF]] guidelines in this regard.

===Singapore===
===South Africa===
South Africa, which has seen a large number of scams related to cryptocurrency, is said to be putting a regulatory timeline in place that will produce a regulatory framework.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2021-06-29/regulatory-clock-ticks-for-cryptocurrency-assets-in-south-africa|title=South Africa Moves to Tighten Crypto Regulation After Scams|date=29 June 2021|access-date=13 July 2021|website=www.bloomberg.com|archive-date=7 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210707023401/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2021-06-29/regulatory-clock-ticks-for-cryptocurrency-assets-in-south-africa|url-status=live}}</ref> The largest scam occurred in April 2021, where the two founders of an African-based cryptocurrency exchange called Africrypt, Raees Cajee and Ameer Cajee, disappeared with $3.8 billion worth of [[bitcoin]].<ref name="regulations">{{cite web|title=South Africa's $4 billion in crypto scams has regulators scrambling to bring in new regulations within the next three to six months|url=https://www.businessinsider.in/cryptocurrency/news/south-africas-4-billion-in-crypto-scams-has-regulators-scrambling-to-bring-in-new-regulations-within-the-next-three-to-six-months/articleshow/84015957.cms|date=1 July 2021|access-date=13 July 2021|website=Business Insider|archive-date=13 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210713103423/https://www.businessinsider.in/cryptocurrency/news/south-africas-4-billion-in-crypto-scams-has-regulators-scrambling-to-bring-in-new-regulations-within-the-next-three-to-six-months/articleshow/84015957.cms|url-status=live}}</ref> Additionally, [[Mirror Trading International]] disappeared with $170 million worth of cryptocurrency in January 2021.<ref name="regulations"/>

===South Korea===
In March 2021, South Korea implemented new legislation to strengthen their oversight of digital assets. This legislation requires all digital asset managers, providers and exchanges to be registered with the Korea Financial Intelligence Unit in order to operate in South Korea.<ref name="thediplomat.com">{{cite web|title=South Korea Tightens Regulations on Cryptocurrencies|url=https://thediplomat.com/2021/07/south-korea-tightens-regulations-on-cryptocurrencies/|date=3 July 2021|access-date=14 July 2021|website=thediplomat.com|archive-date=14 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210714122312/https://thediplomat.com/2021/07/south-korea-tightens-regulations-on-cryptocurrencies/|url-status=live}}</ref> Registering with this unit requires that all exchanges are certified by the Information Security Management System and that they ensure all customers have real name bank accounts. It also requires that the CEO and board members of the exchanges have not been convicted of any crimes and that the exchange holds sufficient levels of deposit insurance to cover losses arising from hacks.<ref name="thediplomat.com"/>

===Switzerland===
Switzerland was one of the first countries to implement the FATF's Travel Rule. FINMA, the Swiss regulator, issued its own guidance to VASPs in 2019. The guidance followed the FATF's Recommendation 16, with stricter requirements. According to FINMA's<ref>{{Cite web |title=FINMA Guidance 02/2019 |url=https://finma.ch/~/media/finma/dokumente/dokumentencenter/myfinma/4dokumentation/finma-aufsichtsmitteilungen/20190826-finma-aufsichtsmitteilung-02-2019.pdf?sc_lang=en |access-date=31 December 2022 |archive-date=14 August 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220814134233/https://www.finma.ch/~/media/finma/dokumente/dokumentencenter/myfinma/4dokumentation/finma-aufsichtsmitteilungen/20190826-finma-aufsichtsmitteilung-02-2019.pdf?sc_lang=en |url-status=live }}</ref> requirements, VASPs need to verify the identity of the beneficiary of the transfer.

===Turkey===
In April 2021, the [[Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey]] banned the use of cryptocurrencies and [[cryptoassets]] for making purchases on the grounds that the use of cryptocurrencies for such payments poses significant transaction risks.<ref>{{cite web|date=28 April 2021|title=No more kebabs for bitcoins as Turkey's crypto-payment ban looms|url=https://www.reuters.com/technology/no-more-kebabs-bitcoins-turkeys-crypto-payment-ban-looms-2021-04-28/|access-date=14 July 2021|website=Reuters|archive-date=14 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210714122309/https://www.reuters.com/technology/no-more-kebabs-bitcoins-turkeys-crypto-payment-ban-looms-2021-04-28/|url-status=live}}</ref>

===United Kingdom===
In the United Kingdom, as of 10 January 2021, all cryptocurrency firms, such as exchanges, advisors and professionals that have either a presence, market product or provide services within the UK market must register with the [[Financial Conduct Authority]]. On 27 June 2021, the financial watchdog demanded that [[Binance]] cease all regulated activities in the UK.<ref name="ft.com">{{Cite news|title=Financial watchdog bans crypto exchange Binance from UK|url=https://www.ft.com/content/8bc0e5e0-2705-496d-a265-acccaffaee87|access-date=12 July 2021|newspaper=Financial Times|date=27 June 2021|last1=Samson|first1=Adam|archive-date=12 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210712022653/https://www.ft.com/content/8bc0e5e0-2705-496d-a265-acccaffaee87|url-status=live}}</ref>

In November 2024, the incoming Labour government confirmed that it will proceed with the regulation of cryptoassets and new UK requirements are expected to come into force in 2026.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.grantthornton.co.uk/insights/the-path-ahead-for-digital-assets-regulation-in-2025/|title=The path ahead for digital assets regulation in 2025|website=Grant Thornton UK LLP}}</ref>

===United States===
In 2021, 17 US states passed laws and resolutions concerning cryptocurrency regulation.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ncsl.org/research/financial-services-and-commerce/cryptocurrency-2021-legislation.aspx |title=Cryptocurrency 2021 Legislation |last=Morton |first=Heather |date=16 December 2021 |access-date=4 January 2021 |work=[[National Conference of State Legislatures]] |archive-date=10 February 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210210222704/https://www.ncsl.org/research/financial-services-and-commerce/cryptocurrency-2021-legislation.aspx |url-status=live }}</ref> This led the Securities and Exchange Commission to start considering what steps to take. On 8 July 2021, [[Elizabeth Warren|Senator Elizabeth Warren]], part of the [[United States Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs|Senate Banking Committee]], wrote to the chairman of the SEC and demanded answers on cryptocurrency regulation due to the increase in cryptocurrency exchange use and the danger this posed to consumers. On 5 August 2021, the chairman, [[Gary Gensler]], responded to Warren's letter and called for legislation focused on "crypto trading, lending and DeFi platforms," because of how vulnerable investors could be when they traded on crypto trading platforms without a broker. He also argued that many tokens in the crypto market may be unregistered securities without required disclosures or market oversight. Additionally, Gensler did not hold back in his criticism of stablecoins. These tokens, which are pegged to the value of fiat currencies, may allow individuals to bypass important public policy goals related to traditional banking and financial systems, such as anti-money laundering, tax compliance, and sanctions.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.protocol.com/fintech/crypto-warren-gensler-sec | title=SEC chair pleads for power to protect crypto investors in 'volatile sector' | last=Pimentel | first=Benjamin | date=11 August 2021 | access-date=2 April 2023 | website=protocol | archive-date=3 April 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230403040815/https://www.protocol.com/fintech/crypto-warren-gensler-sec | url-status=live }}</ref>

On 19 October 2021, the first bitcoin-linked exchange-traded fund (ETF) from [[ProShares]] started trading on the NYSE under the ticker "BITO." [[ProShares]] CEO Michael L. Sapir said the ETF would expose bitcoin to a wider range of investors without the hassle of setting up accounts with cryptocurrency providers. Ian Balina, the CEO of Token Metrics, stated that SEC approval of the ETF was a significant endorsement for the crypto industry because many regulators globally were not in favor of crypto, and retail investors were hesitant to accept crypto. This event would eventually open more opportunities for new capital and new people in this space.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/10/18/first-bitcoin-futures-etf-to-make-its-debut-on-the-nyse-tuesday-proshares-says.html | title=First bitcoin futures ETF to make its debut Tuesday on the NYSE, ProShares says | last=Macheel | first=Tanaya | date=18 October 2021 | access-date=2 April 2023 | website=CNBC | archive-date=3 April 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230403040805/https://www.cnbc.com/2021/10/18/first-bitcoin-futures-etf-to-make-its-debut-on-the-nyse-tuesday-proshares-says.html | url-status=live }}</ref>

The [[United States Department of the Treasury|Department of the Treasury]], on 20 May 2021, announced that it would require any transfer worth $10,000 or more to be reported to the [[Internal Revenue Service]] since cryptocurrency already posed a problem where illegal activity like tax evasion was facilitated broadly. This release from the IRS was a part of efforts to promote better compliance and consider more severe penalties for tax evaders.<ref>{{cite web | last=Franck | first=Thomas | date=20 May 2021 | title=U.S. Treasury calls for stricter cryptocurrency compliance with IRS, says they pose tax evasion risk | website=CNBC |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/05/20/us-treasury-calls-for-stricter-cryptocurrency-compliance-with-irs.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230403040807/https://www.cnbc.com/2021/05/20/us-treasury-calls-for-stricter-cryptocurrency-compliance-with-irs.html | archive-date=3 April 2023 | url-status=live | access-date=2 April 2023 }}</ref>

On 17 February 2022, the [[United States Department of Justice|Department of Justice]] named Eun Young Choi as the first director of a National Cryptocurrency Enforcement Team to help identify and deal with misuse of cryptocurrencies and other digital assets.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2022/2/17/us-justice-department-taps-new-cryptocurrency-czar|title=US Justice Department taps new cryptocurrency czar|website=Aljazeera|access-date=19 February 2022|archive-date=19 February 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220219142640/https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2022/2/17/us-justice-department-taps-new-cryptocurrency-czar|url-status=live}}</ref>

The Biden administration faced a dilemma as it tried to develop regulations for the cryptocurrency industry. On one hand, officials were hesitant to restrict a growing industry. On the other hand, they were committed to preventing illegal cryptocurrency transactions. To reconcile these conflicting goals, on 9 March 2022, Biden issued an executive order.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2022/03/09/executive-order-on-ensuring-responsible-development-of-digital-assets/|title=Executive Order on Ensuring Responsible Development of Digital Assets|date=9 March 2022|access-date=2 April 2023|website=The White House|archive-date=14 March 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220314045129/https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2022/03/09/executive-order-on-ensuring-responsible-development-of-digital-assets/|url-status=live}}</ref> Followed this, on 16 September 2022, the Comprehensive Framework for Responsible Development of Digital Assets document was released<ref>{{cite web|url=https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/09/16/fact-sheet-white-house-releases-first-ever-comprehensive-framework-for-responsible-development-of-digital-assets/|title=FACT SHEET: White House Releases First-Ever Comprehensive Framework for Responsible Development of Digital Assets|date=16 September 2022|access-date=2 April 2023|website=The White House|archive-date=1 April 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230401023659/https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2022/09/16/fact-sheet-white-house-releases-first-ever-comprehensive-framework-for-responsible-development-of-digital-assets/|url-status=live}}</ref> to support development of cryptocurrencies and restrict their illegal use. The executive order included all digital assets, but cryptocurrencies posed both the greatest security risks and potential economic benefits. Though this might not address all of the challenges in crypto industry, it was a significant milestone in the US cryptocurrency regulation history.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.brookings.edu/techstream/the-competing-priorities-facing-u-s-crypto-regulations-bitcoin-ethereum/ | title=The competing priorities facing U.S. crypto regulations | last=Wolff | first=Josephine | date=17 October 2022 | access-date=2 April 2023 | website=Brookings | archive-date=3 April 2023 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230403040807/https://www.brookings.edu/techstream/the-competing-priorities-facing-u-s-crypto-regulations-bitcoin-ethereum/ | url-status=live }}</ref>

In February 2023, the SEC ruled that cryptocurrency exchange [[Kraken (company)|Kraken]]'s estimated $42 billion in staked assets globally operated as an illegal securities seller. The company agreed to a $30 million settlement with the SEC and to cease selling its staking service in the US. The case would impact other major crypto exchanges operating staking programs.<ref>{{Cite news |date=9 February 2023 |title=Crypto Exchange Kraken Ends Staking Program in $30 Million SEC Settlement |language=en |work=Bloomberg.com |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2023-02-09/crypto-exchange-kraken-ends-staking-program-in-sec-settlement |access-date=12 February 2023 |archive-date=24 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230224134003/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2023-02-09/crypto-exchange-kraken-ends-staking-program-in-sec-settlement |url-status=live }}</ref>

On 23 March 2023, the SEC issued an alert to investors stating that firms offering crypto asset securities might not be complying with US laws. The SEC argued that unregistered offerings of crypto asset securities might not include important information.<ref>{{Cite news |date=23 March 2023 |title=US watchdog warns of risks of buying crypto asset securities |language=en |work=Reuters.com |url=https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/us-sec-warns-investors-about-risks-purchasing-crypto-asset-securities-2023-03-23/ |access-date=2 April 2023 |archive-date=2 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230402221010/https://www.reuters.com/business/finance/us-sec-warns-investors-about-risks-purchasing-crypto-asset-securities-2023-03-23/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

On 23 January 2025, President Donald Trump signed [[Executive Order 14178]], ''Strengthening American Leadership in Digital Financial Technology''<ref>{{cite web |title=Strengthening American Leadership in Digital Financial Technology |url=https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/01/31/2025-02123/strengthening-american-leadership-in-digital-financial-technology |website=[[Federal Register]] |access-date=31 January 2025 |date=23 January 2025}}</ref> revoking [[Executive Order 14067]] of 9 March 2022, ''Ensuring Responsible Development of Digital Assets'' and the Department of the Treasury's ''Framework for International Engagement on Digital Assets'' of 7 July 2022.
In addition the order prohibits the establishment, issuance or promotion of [[Central bank digital currency]] and establishes a group tasked with proposing a federal regulatory framework for digital assets within 180 days.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2025/01/president-trump-signs-executive-order-on-digital-assets|title=President Trump Signs Executive Order on Digital Assets &#124; Insights &#124; Holland & Knight|website=www.hklaw.com}}</ref>

==Legality==
{{Main|Legality of cryptocurrency by country or territory}}

The [[Legality of cryptocurrency by country or territory|legal status of cryptocurrencies]] varies substantially from country to country and is still undefined or changing in many of them. At least one study has shown that broad generalizations about the use of bitcoin in illicit finance are significantly overstated and that blockchain analysis is an effective crime fighting and intelligence gathering tool.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Ehrlich |first1=Steven |title=Janet Yellen, Bitcoin And Crypto Fearmongers Get Pushback From Former CIA Director |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/stevenehrlich/2021/04/13/janet-yellen-bitcoin-and-crypto-fearmongers-get-pushback-from-former-cia-director/?sh=1741bd89bb7a |website=Forbes |language=en |access-date=14 April 2021 |archive-date=14 April 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210414164851/https://www.forbes.com/sites/stevenehrlich/2021/04/13/janet-yellen-bitcoin-and-crypto-fearmongers-get-pushback-from-former-cia-director/?sh=1741bd89bb7a |url-status=live }}</ref> While some countries have explicitly allowed their use and trade,<ref>{{Cite news |last=Kharpal |first=Arjun |date=12 April 2017 |title=Bitcoin value rises over $1 billion as Japan, Russia move to legitimize cryptocurrency |publisher=CNBC |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2017/04/12/bitcoin-price-rises-japan-russia-regulation.html |url-status=live |access-date=19 March 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180319214207/https://www.cnbc.com/2017/04/12/bitcoin-price-rises-japan-russia-regulation.html |archive-date=19 March 2018}}</ref> others have banned or restricted it.

According to the&nbsp;[[Library of Congress]]&nbsp;in 2021, an "absolute ban" on trading or using cryptocurrencies applies in 9 countries:
Algeria, Bangladesh, Bolivia, China, Egypt, Iraq, Morocco, Nepal, and the United Arab Emirates. An "implicit ban" applies in another 39 countries or regions, which include: Bahrain, Benin, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Cameroon, Chad, Côte d'Ivoire, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Gabon, Georgia, Guyana, Indonesia, Iran, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Lesotho, Macau, Maldives, Mali, Moldova, Namibia, Niger, Nigeria, Oman, Pakistan, Palau, Republic of Congo, Saudi Arabia, Senegal, Tajikistan, Tanzania, Togo, Turkey, Turkmenistan, Qatar and Vietnam.<ref name="RCAWNov2021LOC">{{cite web |date=November 2021 |title=Regulation of Cryptocurrency Around the World: November 2021 Update |url=https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/llglrd/2021687419/2021687419.pdf |access-date=19 October 2023 |website=Library of Congress |publisher=The Law Library of Congress, Global Legal Research Center |pages=1–61 |archive-date=24 December 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211224043203/https://tile.loc.gov/storage-services/service/ll/llglrd/2021687419/2021687419.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

In the United States and Canada, state and provincial securities regulators, coordinated through the [[North American Securities Administrators Association]], are investigating "Bitcoin scams" and [[Initial coin offering|ICOs]] in 40 jurisdictions.<ref name="WaPo52118">{{Cite news |last=Fung |first=Brian |date=21 May 2018 |title=State regulators unveil nationwide crackdown on suspicious cryptocurrency investment schemes |newspaper=The Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/the-switch/wp/2018/05/21/state-regulators-unveil-nationwide-crackdown-on-suspicious-cryptocurrency-investment-schemes/ |url-status=live |access-date=27 May 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180527081727/https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/the-switch/wp/2018/05/21/state-regulators-unveil-nationwide-crackdown-on-suspicious-cryptocurrency-investment-schemes/ |archive-date=27 May 2018}}</ref>

Various government agencies, departments, and courts have classified bitcoin differently. [[China Central Bank]] banned the handling of bitcoins by financial institutions in [[China]] in early 2014.

In Russia, though owning cryptocurrency is legal, its residents are only allowed to purchase goods from other residents using the [[Russian ruble]] while nonresidents are allowed to use foreign currency.<ref>[https://www.forbes.com/sites/kashmirhill/2014/01/31/bitcoins-legality-around-the-world/ Bitcoin's Legality Around The World] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170916060759/https://www.forbes.com/sites/kashmirhill/2014/01/31/bitcoins-legality-around-the-world/ |date=16 September 2017 }}, Forbes, 31 January 2014</ref> Regulations and bans that apply to bitcoin probably extend to similar cryptocurrency systems.<ref>{{Cite SSRN |last=Tasca |first=Paolo |date=7 September 2015 |title=Digital Currencies: Principles, Trends, Opportunities, and Risks |ssrn=2657598}}</ref>

In August 2018, the [[Bank of Thailand]] announced its plans to create its own cryptocurrency, the Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC).<ref>{{Cite news |last=Thompson |first=Luke |date=24 August 2018 |title=Bank of Thailand to launch its own crypto-currency |work=Asia Times |url=https://asiatimes.com/2018/08/amputee-in-taiwan-gets-new-3d-printed-prosthetic/ |access-date=27 August 2018 |archive-date=28 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240628094543/https://widgets.outbrain.com/nanoWidget/externals/topics/topics.html?r=https%3A%2F%2Fasiatimes.com |url-status=live }}</ref>
