* [[Yandex]]<ref name=":3">{{Cite news |last=Wilson |first=Thomas |date=28 March 2018 |title=Twitter and LinkedIn ban cryptocurrency adverts – leaving regulators behind |work=Independent |agency=[[Reuters]] |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/business/analysis-and-features/twitter-ban-cryptocurrency-adverts-regulators-bitcoin-facebook-social-media-a8277176.html |url-status=live |access-date=3 April 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180404074502/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/business/analysis-and-features/twitter-ban-cryptocurrency-adverts-regulators-bitcoin-facebook-social-media-a8277176.html |archive-date=4 April 2018}}</ref>

===U.S. tax status===
In March 2014, the United States [[Internal Revenue Service]] (IRS) ruled that bitcoin will be treated as property for tax purposes. Therefore, virtual currencies are considered commodities subject to capital gains tax.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Schaub |first1=Mark |last2=Phares |first2=H. Banker |date=15 August 2020 |title=Cryptocurrency value changes in response to national elections: do they behave like money or commodities? |journal=Applied Economics Letters |volume=27 |issue=14 |pages=1135–1140 |doi=10.1080/13504851.2019.1673297 }}</ref>

===Legal concerns relating to an unregulated global economy===
As the popularity and demand for cryptocurrencies has increased,<ref>{{Cite SSRN |last1=Iwamura |first1=Mitsuru |last2=Kitamura |first2=Yukinobu |last3=Matsumoto |first3=Tsutomu |date=28 February 2014 |title=Is Bitcoin the Only Cryptocurrency in the Town? Economics of Cryptocurrency and Friedrich A. Hayek |ssrn=2405790 }}</ref> so have concerns that they offer an unregulated person-to-person global economy that may become a threat to society. Concerns abound that they may become tools for anonymous web criminals.<ref name=":1">Ali, S, T; Clarke, D; McCorry, P; Bitcoin: Perils of an Unregulated Global P2P Currency. Newcastle upon Tyne: Newcastle University: Computing Science, 2015. Technical Report Series, No. CS-TR-1470</ref>

Cryptocurrency networks display a lack of regulation that has been criticized as enabling criminals who seek to evade taxes and [[Money laundering|launder money]]. Money laundering issues [[FinCEN Files|are also present in regular bank transfers]], however with bank-to-bank wire transfers for instance, the account holder must [[Wire transfer#Security|provide a proven identity]].

Transactions that occur through the use and exchange of these cryptocurrencies are independent from formal banking systems, and therefore can make tax evasion simpler for individuals. Since charting taxable income is based upon what a recipient reports to the revenue service, it becomes extremely difficult to account for transactions made using cryptocurrencies, a mode of exchange that is complex and difficult to track.<ref name=":1" />

Systems of anonymity that most cryptocurrencies offer can also serve as a means to launder money. Rather than laundering money through an intricate network of financial actors and [[offshore bank account]]s, laundering money through cryptocurrencies can be achieved through anonymous transactions.<ref name=":1" />

Cryptocurrency makes legal enforcement against extremist groups more complicated, which consequently strengthens them.<ref name="fortune_supremacists_2022">{{cite web |title=How white supremacists and the far right use Bitcoin to evade the law and get rich |url=https://fortune.com/2021/09/28/currency-of-alt-right-how-white-supremacists-and-far-right-use-bitcoin/ |access-date=1 March 2022 |website=Fortune |language=en |archive-date=1 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220301210303/https://fortune.com/2021/09/28/currency-of-alt-right-how-white-supremacists-and-far-right-use-bitcoin/ |url-status=live }}</ref> [[White supremacist]] [[Richard B. Spencer|Richard Spencer]] declared bitcoin the "currency of the [[alt-right]]".<ref name="fortune_supremacists_2022" />

===Loss, theft, and fraud===
{{Main|Cryptocurrency and crime}}

In February 2014, the world's largest bitcoin exchange, [[Mt. Gox]], declared [[bankruptcy]]. Likely due to theft, the company claimed that it had lost nearly 750,000 bitcoins belonging to their clients. This added up to approximately 7% of all bitcoins in existence, worth a total of $473 million. Mt. Gox blamed hackers, who had exploited the [[transaction malleability problem]]s in the network. The price of a bitcoin fell from a high of about $1,160 in December to under $400 in February.<ref>[https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2014-02-28/mt-gox-exchange-files-for-bankruptcy.html Mt. Gox Seeks Bankruptcy After $480 Million Bitcoin Loss] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150112234804/http://www.bloomberg.com/news/2014-02-28/mt-gox-exchange-files-for-bankruptcy.html |date=12 January 2015 }}, Carter Dougherty and Grace Huang, Bloomberg News, 28 February 2014</ref>

On 21 November 2017, [[Tether (cryptocurrency)|Tether]] announced that it had been hacked, losing $31 million in USDT from its core treasury wallet.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Russell |first=Jon |title=Tether, a startup that works with bitcoin exchanges, claims a hacker stole&nbsp;$31M |work=TechCrunch |url=https://techcrunch.com/2017/11/20/tether-claims-a-hacker-stole-31m/ |url-status=live |access-date=22 November 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171121105158/https://techcrunch.com/2017/11/20/tether-claims-a-hacker-stole-31m/ |archive-date=21 November 2017}}</ref>

On 7 December 2017, Slovenian cryptocurrency exchange [[NiceHash|Nicehash]] reported that hackers had stolen over $70 million using a hijacked company computer.<ref>{{cite web |last=Iyengar |first=Rishi |date=7 December 2017 |title=More than $70 million stolen in bitcoin hack |url=https://money.cnn.com/2017/12/07/technology/nicehash-bitcoin-theft-hacking/index.html |access-date=2 March 2022 |website=CNNMoney |archive-date=20 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220920091520/https://money.cnn.com/2017/12/07/technology/nicehash-bitcoin-theft-hacking/index.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

On 19 December 2017, Yapian, the owner of South Korean exchange Youbit, filed for bankruptcy after suffering two hacks that year.<ref>{{cite web |last=Haselton |first=Todd |date=19 December 2017 |title=A South Korean cryptocurrency exchange files for bankruptcy after hack, says users will get 75% of assets for now |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2017/12/19/yapian-youbit-exchange-files-bankruptcy.html |access-date=2 March 2022 |website=CNBC |archive-date=6 September 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220906124744/https://www.cnbc.com/2017/12/19/yapian-youbit-exchange-files-bankruptcy.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=19 December 2017 |title=South Korean cryptocurrency exchange to file for bankruptcy after hacking |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-bitcoin-exchange-southkorea-idUSKBN1ED0NJ |access-date=2 March 2022 |archive-date=28 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220528053057/https://www.reuters.com/article/us-bitcoin-exchange-southkorea-idUSKBN1ED0NJ |url-status=live }}</ref> Customers were still granted access to 75% of their assets.

In May 2018, [[Bitcoin Gold]] had its transactions hijacked and abused by unknown hackers.<ref>{{cite web |last=Cimpanu |first=Catalin |date=4 September 2018 |title=Bitcoin Gold delisted from major cryptocurrency exchange after refusing to pay hack damages |url=https://www.zdnet.com/article/bitcoin-gold-delisted-from-major-cryptocurrency-exchange-after-refusing-to-pay-hack-damages/ |website=ZDNet |language=en |access-date=11 February 2020 |archive-date=24 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220524122220/https://www.zdnet.com/article/bitcoin-gold-delisted-from-major-cryptocurrency-exchange-after-refusing-to-pay-hack-damages/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Exchanges lost an estimated $18m and bitcoin Gold was delisted from Bittrex after it refused to pay its share of the damages.

On 13 September 2018, Homero Josh Garza was sentenced to 21 months of imprisonment, followed by three years of supervised release.<ref>{{cite web |date=13 September 2018 |title=Former Virtual Currency CEO Involved in $9 Million Fraud Scheme Sentenced to Prison |url=https://www.justice.gov/usao-ct/pr/former-virtual-currency-ceo-involved-9-million-fraud-scheme-sentenced-prison |access-date=2 March 2022 |website=www.justice.gov |language=en |archive-date=2 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220302104750/https://www.justice.gov/usao-ct/pr/former-virtual-currency-ceo-involved-9-million-fraud-scheme-sentenced-prison |url-status=live }}</ref> Garza had founded the cryptocurrency startups GAW Miners and ZenMiner in 2014, acknowledged in a [[plea agreement]] that the companies were part of a [[pyramid scheme]], and pleaded guilty to [[wire fraud]] in 2015. The SEC separately brought a civil enforcement action in the US against Garza, who was eventually ordered to pay a judgment of $9.1 million plus $700,000 in interest. The SEC's complaint stated that Garza, through his companies, had fraudulently sold "investment contracts representing shares in the profits they claimed would be generated" from mining.<ref>Cyris Farivar, [https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2017/10/bitcoin-fraudster-hit-with-9-1m-civil-judgment-on-top-of-criminal-guilty-plea/ GAW Miners founder owes nearly $10 million to SEC over Bitcoin fraud] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171229112405/https://arstechnica.com/tech-policy/2017/10/bitcoin-fraudster-hit-with-9-1m-civil-judgment-on-top-of-criminal-guilty-plea/|date=29 December 2017}}, ''Ars Technica'' (5 October 2017).</ref>

In January 2018, Japanese exchange [[Coincheck]] reported that hackers had stolen cryptocurrency worth $530 million.<ref>{{cite web |last=Shane |first=Daniel |date=29 January 2018 |title=$530 million cryptocurrency heist may be biggest ever |url=https://money.cnn.com/2018/01/29/technology/coincheck-cryptocurrency-exchange-hack-japan/index.html |access-date=2 March 2022 |website=CNNMoney |archive-date=15 August 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190815202041/https://money.cnn.com/2018/01/29/technology/coincheck-cryptocurrency-exchange-hack-japan/index.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In June 2018, South Korean exchange Coinrail was hacked, losing over $37 million in crypto.<ref>{{cite web |last=Shane |first=Daniel |date=11 June 2018 |title=Billions in cryptocurrency wealth wiped out after hack |url=https://money.cnn.com/2018/06/11/investing/coinrail-hack-bitcoin-exchange/index.html |access-date=2 March 2022 |website=CNNMoney |archive-date=11 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180711032051/https://money.cnn.com/2018/06/11/investing/coinrail-hack-bitcoin-exchange/index.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> The hack worsened a cryptocurrency selloff by an additional $42 billion.<ref>{{Citation |first1=Eric |last1=Lam |first2=Jiyeun |last2=Lee |first3=Jordan |last3=Robertson |title=Cryptocurrencies Lose $42 Billion After South Korean Bourse Hack |date=10 June 2018 |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-06-10/bitcoin-tumbles-most-in-two-weeks-amid-south-korea-exchange-hack |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180612005144/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2018-06-10/bitcoin-tumbles-most-in-two-weeks-amid-south-korea-exchange-hack |publisher=[[Bloomberg News]] |access-date=12 June 2018 |archive-date=12 June 2018 |url-status=live}}</ref>

On 9 July 2018, the exchange Bancor, whose code and fundraising had been subjects of controversy, had $23.5 million in crypto stolen.<ref name="Bancorhack">{{Cite news |last=Roberts |first=Jeff John |date=9 July 2018 |title=Another Crypto Fail: Hackers Steal $23.5 Million from Token Service Bancor |work=Fortune |url=http://fortune.com/2018/07/09/bancor-hack/ |url-status=live |access-date=10 July 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180710013104/http://fortune.com/2018/07/09/bancor-hack/ |archive-date=10 July 2018}}</ref>

A 2020 EU report found that users had lost crypto-assets worth hundreds of millions of US dollars in security breaches at exchanges and storage providers. Between 2011 and 2019, reported breaches ranged from four to twelve a year. In 2019, more than a billion dollars' worth of cryptoassets was reported stolen. Stolen assets "typically find their way to illegal markets and are used to fund further criminal activity".<ref>{{citation |first1=Robby |last1=Houben |first2=Alexander |last2=Snyers |date=April 2020 |title=Crypto-assets: Key developments, regulatory concerns and responses |publisher=EU Directorate-General for Internal Policies |url=https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/STUD/2020/648779/IPOL_STU(2020)648779_EN.pdf |access-date=16 July 2021 |archive-date=16 July 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210716211640/https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/STUD/2020/648779/IPOL_STU(2020)648779_EN.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

According to a 2020 report produced by the [[United States Attorney General]]'s Cyber-Digital Task Force, three categories make up the majority of illicit cryptocurrency uses: "(1) financial transactions associated with the commission of crimes; (2) [[money laundering]] and the [[Tax evasion|shielding of legitimate activity from tax]], reporting, or other legal requirements; or (3) crimes, such as theft, directly implicating the cryptocurrency marketplace itself." The report concluded that "for cryptocurrency to realize its truly transformative potential, it is imperative that these risks be addressed" and that "the government has legal and regulatory tools available at its disposal to confront the threats posed by cryptocurrency's illicit uses".<ref>{{cite web|date=8 October 2020|title=Attorney General William P. Barr Announces Publication of Cryptocurrency Enforcement Framework|url=https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/attorney-general-william-p-barr-announces-publication-cryptocurrency-enforcement-framework|access-date=17 January 2022|website=www.justice.gov|archive-date=17 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220117092747/https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/attorney-general-william-p-barr-announces-publication-cryptocurrency-enforcement-framework|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=DOJ Releases Cryptocurrency Enforcement Report|url=https://www.natlawreview.com/article/doj-releases-cryptocurrency-enforcement-report|access-date=17 January 2022|website=The National Law Review|archive-date=17 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220117093115/https://www.natlawreview.com/article/doj-releases-cryptocurrency-enforcement-report|url-status=live}}</ref>

According to the UK 2020 national risk assessment—a comprehensive assessment of money laundering and terrorist financing risk in the UK—the risk of using cryptoassets such as bitcoin for money laundering and terrorism financing is assessed as "medium" (from "low" in the previous 2017 report).<ref>{{cite web|title=National risk assessment of money laundering and terrorist financing 2020|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-risk-assessment-of-money-laundering-and-terrorist-financing-2020|access-date=17 January 2022|website=GOV.UK|language=en|archive-date=18 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220118182353/https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-risk-assessment-of-money-laundering-and-terrorist-financing-2020|url-status=live}}</ref> Legal scholars suggested that the money laundering opportunities may be more perceived than real.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Campbell-Verduyn |first1=Malcolm |title=Bitcoin, crypto-coins, and global anti-money laundering governance |journal=Crime, Law and Social Change |date=March 2018 |volume=69 |issue=2 |pages=283–305 |doi=10.1007/s10611-017-9756-5 }}</ref> [[Blockchain analysis]] company Chainalysis concluded that illicit activities like [[cybercrime]], [[money laundering]] and [[terrorism financing]] made up only 0.15% of all crypto transactions conducted in 2021, representing a total of $14 billion.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.axios.com/2022/01/06/cryptocurrency-scam-crime-popularity-report | title=Report: Illicit activity actually a tiny part of cryptocurrency use | date=6 January 2022 | access-date=23 August 2022 | archive-date=23 August 2022 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220823124144/https://www.axios.com/2022/01/06/cryptocurrency-scam-crime-popularity-report | url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last1=Sun|first1=Mengqi|last2=Smagalla|first2=David|date=6 January 2022|title=Cryptocurrency-Based Crime Hit a Record $14 Billion in 2021|language=en-US|work=[[The Wall Street Journal]]|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/cryptocurrency-based-crime-hit-a-record-14-billion-in-2021-11641500073|access-date=16 January 2022|issn=0099-9660|archive-date=7 October 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221007151053/https://www.wsj.com/articles/cryptocurrency-based-crime-hit-a-record-14-billion-in-2021-11641500073|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date=6 January 2022|title=Crypto Crime Trends for 2022: Illicit Transaction Activity Reaches All-Time High in Value, All-Time Low in Share of All Cryptocurrency Activity|url=https://blog.chainalysis.com/reports/2022-crypto-crime-report-introduction/|access-date=16 January 2022|website=Chainalysis|language=en-US|archive-date=15 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220115103636/https://blog.chainalysis.com/reports/2022-crypto-crime-report-introduction/|url-status=live}}</ref>

In December 2021, Monkey Kingdom, a NFT project based in Hong Kong, lost US$1.3 million worth of cryptocurrencies via a phishing link used by the hacker.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-trends/article/3160707/hot-hong-kong-nft-project-monkey-kingdom-loses-us13-million-hack |title=Hot Hong Kong NFT project Monkey Kingdom loses US$1.3 million in hack, exposing security concerns |last=Ye |first=Josh |work=SCMP |date=22 December 2021 |access-date=13 April 2022 |archive-date=13 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220413032828/https://www.scmp.com/tech/tech-trends/article/3160707/hot-hong-kong-nft-project-monkey-kingdom-loses-us13-million-hack |url-status=live }}</ref>

On 2 November 2023, [[Sam Bankman-Fried]] was pronounced guilty on seven counts of fraud related to [[FTX]].<ref name="cnbc-guilty">{{Cite web |last=Sigalos |first=MacKenzie |date=2 November 2023 |title=Sam Bankman-Fried found guilty on all seven criminal fraud counts |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2023/11/02/sam-bankman-fried-found-guilty-on-all-seven-criminal-fraud-counts.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231103011927/https://www.cnbc.com/2023/11/02/sam-bankman-fried-found-guilty-on-all-seven-criminal-fraud-counts.html |archive-date=3 November 2023 |access-date=3 November 2023 |website=CNBC}}</ref> Federal criminal court sentencing experts speculated on the potential amount of prison time likely to be meted out.<ref name="Livni">{{Cite news |last1=Livni |first1=Ephrat |last2=Warner |first2=Bernhard |date=11 November 2023 |title=Sam Bankman-Fried Could Get 100 Years in Prison. What Is Fair? |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url-access=subscription |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/11/11/business/dealbook/sam-bankman-fried-sentencing.html |access-date=16 November 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=29 February 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240229233927/https://www.nytimes.com/2023/11/11/business/dealbook/sam-bankman-fried-sentencing.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="Clifford">{{cite news |last1=Clifford |first1=Stephanie |title=Sam Bankman-Fried's trial has ended, but the fallout has just begun |url=https://www.fastcompany.com/90977987/sam-bankman-fried-trial-fallout-has-just-begun |access-date=15 November 2023 |work=Fast Company |date=8 November 2023 |archive-date=15 November 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231115084301/https://www.fastcompany.com/90977987/sam-bankman-fried-trial-fallout-has-just-begun |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Bultman |first=Matthew |date=2 November 2023 |title=Bankman-Fried's Pre-Trial Antics Haunt Him Before Sentencing (1) |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/securities-law/bankman-frieds-pre-trial-antics-haunt-him-before-sentencing-1 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://archive.today/20231105015427/https://news.bloomberglaw.com/securities-law/bankman-frieds-pre-trial-antics-haunt-him-before-sentencing-1 |archive-date=5 November 2023 |access-date=20 February 2024 |website=[[Bloomberg Law]] |language=en |quote=Former federal prosecutors predict the fallen FTX co-founder will receive at least 20 years in prison. At the high end, federal sentencing guidelines could recommend what equates to a life sentence for Bankman-Fried, who turned 31 in March. District Judge Lewis A. Kaplan has been critical of the guidelines and often imposed more lenient sentences in previous cases before his court.}}</ref> On 28 March 2024, the court sentenced Bankman-Fried to 25 years in prison.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Ramey |first=James Fanelli and Corinne |title=FTX Founder Sam Bankman-Fried Sentenced to 25 Years |url=https://www.wsj.com/finance/currencies/sam-bankman-fried-sentencing-ftx-fraud-2d92fce9 |access-date=28 March 2024 |work=[[The Wall Street Journal]] |url-access=subscription |language=en-US |archive-date=24 April 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240424005115/https://www.wsj.com/finance/currencies/sam-bankman-fried-sentencing-ftx-fraud-2d92fce9 |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Money laundering===
{{See also|Cryptocurrency and crime}}

According to blockchain data company [[Chainalysis]], criminals laundered $8.6 billion worth of cryptocurrency in 2021, up 30% from the previous year.<ref>{{Cite news |date=26 January 2022 |title=Crypto money laundering rises 30%, report finds |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-60072195 |access-date=2 March 2022 |archive-date=1 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220301112734/https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-60072195 |url-status=live }}</ref> The data suggests that rather than managing numerous illicit havens, cybercriminals make use of a small group of purpose-built centralized exchanges for sending and receiving illicit cryptocurrency. In 2021, those exchanges received 47% of funds sent by crime-linked addresses.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sackey |first1=Andrew |last2=Shah |first2=Hinesh |date=4 February 2022 |title=Cryptocurrency money laundering on DeFi skyrockets |url=https://www.pinsentmasons.com/out-law/analysis/cryptocurrency-money-laundering-on-defi-skyrockets |access-date=2 March 2022 |website=Pinsent Masons |language=en-GB |archive-date=2 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220302173858/https://www.pinsentmasons.com/out-law/analysis/cryptocurrency-money-laundering-on-defi-skyrockets |url-status=live }}</ref> Almost $2.2 billion worth of cryptocurrencies was embezzled from [[decentralized finance]] protocols in 2021, which represents 72% of all cryptocurrency theft in 2021.{{Citation needed|date=December 2025}}

According to ''Bloomberg'' and the ''New York Times'', Federation Tower, a complex in the heart of Moscow, is home to many cryptocurrency businesses under suspicion of facilitating extensive money laundering, including accepting illicit cryptocurrency funds obtained through scams, [[darknet market]]s, and [[ransomware]].<ref name=":0">{{cite web |date=14 February 2022 |title=Russian Cybercriminals Drive Significant Ransomware and Cryptocurrency-based Money Laundering Activity |url=https://blog.chainalysis.com/reports/2022-crypto-crime-report-preview-russia-ransomware-money-laundering/ |access-date=2 March 2022 |website=Chainalysis |language=en-US |archive-date=3 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220303033347/https://blog.chainalysis.com/reports/2022-crypto-crime-report-preview-russia-ransomware-money-laundering/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Notable businesses include [[Garantex]],<ref>{{cite web |last=Bergwick |first=Angus |title=The Crypto Exchange Moving Money for Criminal Gangs, Rich Russians and a Hamas-Linked Terror Group |url=https://www.wsj.com/finance/currencies/garantex-russian-crypto-hamas-crime-sanctions-a3648357 |publisher=The Wall Street Journal |date=13 October 2023 |access-date=24 October 2023 |archive-date=24 October 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231024213701/https://www.wsj.com/finance/currencies/garantex-russian-crypto-hamas-crime-sanctions-a3648357 |url-status=live }}</ref> Eggchange, Cashbank, Buy-Bitcoin, Tetchange, Bitzlato, and Suex, which was sanctioned by the U.S. in 2021. Bitzlato founder and owner Anatoly Legkodymov was arrested following money-laundering charges by the United States Department of Justice.<ref>{{Cite web |date=18 January 2023 |title=Founder and Majority Owner of Bitzlato, a Cryptocurrency Exchange, Charged with Unlicensed Money Transmitting |url=https://www.justice.gov/usao-edny/pr/founder-and-majority-owner-bitzlato-cryptocurrency-exchange-charged-unlicensed-money |access-date=18 January 2023 |website=www.justice.gov |language=en |archive-date=18 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230118172451/https://www.justice.gov/usao-edny/pr/founder-and-majority-owner-bitzlato-cryptocurrency-exchange-charged-unlicensed-money |url-status=live }}</ref>

Dark money has also been flowing into Russia through a dark web marketplace called Hydra, which is powered by cryptocurrency, and enjoyed more than $1 billion in sales in 2020, according to Chainalysis.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Flitter |first1=Emily |last2=Yaffe-Bellany |first2=David |date=23 February 2022 |title=Russia Could Use Cryptocurrency to Blunt the Force of U.S. Sanctions |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/02/23/business/russia-sanctions-cryptocurrency.html |access-date=2 March 2022 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=1 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220301145413/https://www.nytimes.com/2022/02/23/business/russia-sanctions-cryptocurrency.html |url-status=live }}</ref> The platform demands that sellers liquidate cryptocurrency only through certain regional exchanges, which has made it difficult for investigators to trace the money.{{Citation needed|date=December 2025}}

Almost 74% of ransomware revenue in 2021 — over $400 million worth of cryptocurrency — went to software strains likely affiliated with Russia, where oversight is notoriously limited.<ref name=":0" /> However, Russians are also leaders in the benign adoption of cryptocurrencies, as the ruble is unreliable, and [[Vladimir Putin|President Putin]] favours the idea of "overcoming the excessive domination of the limited number of reserve currencies."<ref>{{cite web |last=Matthews |first=Owen |date=18 September 2017 |title=Why Russia is finally embracing virtual currencies. Hint: It rhymes with honey wandering |url=https://www.newsweek.com/russia-finally-embracing-virtual-currencies-666794 |access-date=2 March 2022 |website=Newsweek |language=en |archive-date=2 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220302173856/https://www.newsweek.com/russia-finally-embracing-virtual-currencies-666794 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2022, RenBridge—an unregulated alternative to exchanges for transferring value between blockchains—was found to be responsible for the laundering of at least $540 million since 2020. It is especially popular with people attempting to launder money from theft. This includes a cyberattack on Japanese crypto exchange Liquid that has been linked to [[North Korea]].<ref>{{cite web |date=8 October 2022 |title=Cross-chain Crime: More Than Half a Billion Dollars has Been Laundered Through a Cross-chain Bridge |url=https://hub.elliptic.co/analysis/cross-chain-crime-more-than-half-a-billion-dollars-has-been-laundered-through-a-cross-chain-bridge/ |work=Elliptic Connect |access-date=2 April 2023 |language=en |archive-date=2 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230402231810/https://hub.elliptic.co/analysis/cross-chain-crime-more-than-half-a-billion-dollars-has-been-laundered-through-a-cross-chain-bridge/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Darknet markets===
{{Main|Darknet market}}

Properties of cryptocurrencies gave them popularity in applications such as a safe haven in banking crises and means of payment, which also led to the cryptocurrency use in controversial settings in the form of [[darknet market|online black markets]], such as [[Silk Road (marketplace)|Silk Road]].<ref name=":1" /> The original Silk Road was shut down in October 2013 and there have been two more versions in use since then. In the year following the initial shutdown of Silk Road, the number of prominent dark markets increased from four to twelve, while the amount of drug listings increased from 18,000 to 32,000.<ref name=":1" />

Darknet markets present challenges in regard to their legality. Cryptocurrency used in dark markets are not clearly or legally classified in almost all parts of the world. In the US, bitcoins are regarded as "virtual assets".{{citation needed|date=November 2019}} This type of ambiguous classification puts pressure on law enforcement agencies around the world to adapt to the shifting drug trade of dark markets.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Raeesi |first=Reza |date=23 April 2015 |title=The Silk Road, Bitcoins and the Global Prohibition Regime on the International Trade in Illicit Drugs: Can this Storm Be Weathered? |url=http://gjis.journals.yorku.ca/index.php/gjis/article/view/38935 |url-status=live |journal=Glendon Journal of International Studies / Revue d'Études Internationales de Glendon |volume=8 |issue=1–2 |issn=2291-3920 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151222084405/http://gjis.journals.yorku.ca/index.php/gjis/article/view/38935 |archive-date=22 December 2015}}</ref>{{unreliable source?|date=November 2019}}

===Wash trades===
Various studies have found that crypto-trading is rife with [[Wash trade|wash trading]], a process, illegal in some jurisdictions, involving buyers and sellers being the same person or group, and which may be used to manipulate the price of a cryptocurrency or inflate volume artificially. Exchanges with higher volumes can demand higher premiums from token issuers.<ref name=":4">{{cite web |title=Six Months After Bitwise, Wash Trading Lives on in Crypto {{!}} Finance Magnates |url=https://www.financemagnates.com/cryptocurrency/news/things-are-better-but-wash-trading-persists-in-crypto-heres-why/ |access-date=3 March 2022 |website=Financial and Business News {{!}} Finance Magnates |date=25 September 2019 |language=en |archive-date=3 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220303123444/https://www.financemagnates.com/cryptocurrency/news/things-are-better-but-wash-trading-persists-in-crypto-heres-why/ |url-status=live }}</ref> A study from 2019 concluded that up to 80% of trades on unregulated cryptocurrency exchanges could be wash trades.<ref name=":4" /> A 2019 report by Bitwise Asset Management claimed that 95% of all bitcoin trading volume reported on major website CoinMarketCap had been artificially generated, and of 81 exchanges studied, only 10 provided legitimate volume figures.<ref>{{cite web |last=Bovaird |first=Charles |title=95% Of Reported Bitcoin Trading Volume Is Fake, Says Bitwise |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/cbovaird/2019/03/22/95-of-reported-bitcoin-trading-volume-is-fake-says-bitwise/ |access-date=3 March 2022 |website=Forbes |language=en |archive-date=3 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220303123439/https://www.forbes.com/sites/cbovaird/2019/03/22/95-of-reported-bitcoin-trading-volume-is-fake-says-bitwise/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

===As a tool to evade sanctions===
In 2022, cryptocurrencies attracted attention when Western nations imposed severe economic sanctions on Russia in the aftermath of [[2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine|its invasion of Ukraine]] in February. However, American sources warned in March that some crypto-transactions could potentially be used to evade economic sanctions against Russia and Belarus.<ref>[https://www.wsj.com/articles/u-s-warns-banks-crypto-firms-against-potential-efforts-to-evade-russian-sanctions-11646696802 U.S. Warns Banks, Crypto Firms Against Potential Efforts to Evade Russian Sanctions] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220310023714/https://www.wsj.com/articles/u-s-warns-banks-crypto-firms-against-potential-efforts-to-evade-russian-sanctions-11646696802 |date=10 March 2022 }} (9 March 2022) ''www.wsj.com''. Retrieved 9 March 2022.</ref>

In April 2022, the computer programmer [[Virgil Griffith]] received a five-year prison sentence in the US for attending a Pyongyang cryptocurrency conference, where he gave a presentation on blockchains which might be used for sanctions evasion.<ref>{{Cite news |date=13 April 2022 |title=US cryptocurrency expert jailed for helping North Korea evade sanctions |language=en-GB |work=BBC News |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/business-61090064 |access-date=14 May 2022 |archive-date=14 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220514131633/https://www.bbc.com/news/business-61090064 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Impacts and analysis==
{{external media | width = 210px | float = right | video1 = [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vo6s1mUjxQQ Cryptocurrencies: looking beyond the hype], [[Hyun Song Shin]], [[Bank for International Settlements]], 2:48<ref name="bis report" /> }}

The [[Bank for International Settlements]] summarized several criticisms of cryptocurrencies in Chapter V of their 2018 annual report. The criticisms include the lack of stability in their price, the high energy consumption, high and variable transactions costs, the poor security and fraud at cryptocurrency exchanges, vulnerability to debasement (from forking), and the influence of miners.<ref name="bis report">{{cite news |last=Janda |first=Michael |date=18 June 2018 |title=Cryptocurrencies like bitcoin cannot replace money, says Bank for International Settlements |publisher=ABC (Australia) |url=http://www.abc.net.au/news/2018-06-18/cryptocurrencies-cannot-replace-money-bis/9879448 |url-status=live |access-date=18 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180618072225/http://www.abc.net.au/news/2018-06-18/cryptocurrencies-cannot-replace-money-bis/9879448 |archive-date=18 June 2018}}</ref><ref name="chapterV">{{cite web |last=Hyun Song Shin |date=June 2018 |title=Chapter V. Cryptocurrencies: looking beyond the hype |url=https://www.bis.org/publ/arpdf/ar2018e5.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180618080358/https://www.bis.org/publ/arpdf/ar2018e5.pdf |archive-date=18 June 2018 |access-date=19 June 2018 |website=BIS 2018 Annual Economic Report |publisher=Bank for International Settlements |quote=Put in the simplest terms, the quest for decentralised trust has quickly become an environmental disaster.}}</ref><ref name="LATHiltzik">{{Cite news |last=Hiltzik |first=Michael |date=18 June 2018 |title=Is this scathing report the death knell for bitcoin? |work=Los Angeles Times |url=https://www.latimes.com/business/hiltzik/la-fi-hiltzik-bitcoin-bank-20180618-story.html |url-status=live |access-date=19 June 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180618233532/http://www.latimes.com/business/hiltzik/la-fi-hiltzik-bitcoin-bank-20180618-story.html |archive-date=18 June 2018}}</ref>

===Speculation, fraud, and adoption===
{{See also|Cryptocurrency bubble|Cryptocurrency and crime|Bitcoin network|label 3=Criminal activity on Bitcoin's network}}

Cryptocurrencies have been compared to [[Ponzi schemes]], [[pyramid scheme]]s<ref>{{cite web |last=Polgar |first=David |title=Cryptocurrency is a giant multi-level marketing scheme |url=https://qz.com/1217460/cryptocurrency-is-a-giant-multi-level-marketing-scheme/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180301150230/https://qz.com/1217460/cryptocurrency-is-a-giant-multi-level-marketing-scheme/ |archive-date=1 March 2018 |access-date=2 March 2018 |website=Quartz |date=28 February 2018 |publisher=Quartz Media LLC}}</ref> and [[economic bubble]]s,<ref>{{cite report |last1=Chohan |first1=Usman W. |date=19 December 2017 |title=Bitcoins and Bank Runs: Analysis of Market Imperfections and Investor Hysterics |ssrn=3090405 }}</ref> such as [[housing market bubble]]s.<ref>{{Citation |last=McCrum |first=Dan |title=Bitcoin's place in the long history of pyramid schemes |date=10 November 2015 |url=https://www.ft.com/content/1877c388-8797-11e5-90de-f44762bf9896 |work=Financial Times |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170323054631/https://www.ft.com/content/1877c388-8797-11e5-90de-f44762bf9896 |archive-date=23 March 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref> [[Howard Marks (investor)|Howard Marks]] of [[Oaktree Capital Management]] stated in 2017 that digital currencies were "nothing but an unfounded fad (or perhaps even a pyramid scheme), based on a willingness to ascribe value to something that has little or none beyond what people will pay for it", and compared them to the [[tulip mania]] (1637), [[South Sea Bubble]] (1720), and [[dot-com bubble]] (1999), which all experienced profound price booms and busts.<ref>{{Citation |last=Kim |first=Tae |title=Billionaire investor Marks, who called the dotcom bubble, says bitcoin is a 'pyramid scheme' |date=27 July 2017 |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2017/07/26/billionaire-investor-marks-who-called-the-dotcom-bubble-says-bitcoin-is-a-pyramid-scheme.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170905042046/https://www.cnbc.com/2017/07/26/billionaire-investor-marks-who-called-the-dotcom-bubble-says-bitcoin-is-a-pyramid-scheme.html |publisher=CNBC |archive-date=5 September 2017 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Regulators in several countries have warned against cryptocurrency and some have taken measures to dissuade users.<ref>{{cite web |last=Schwartzkopff |first=Frances |date=17 December 2013 |title=Bitcoins Spark Regulatory Crackdown as Denmark Drafts Rules |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2013-12-17/bitcoin-rules-drafted-in-denmark-as-regulator-warns-against-use.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131229064125/http://www.bloomberg.com/news/2013-12-17/bitcoin-rules-drafted-in-denmark-as-regulator-warns-against-use.html |archive-date=29 December 2013 |access-date=29 December 2013 |publisher=Bloomberg}}</ref> However, research in 2021 by the UK's financial regulator suggests such warnings either went unheard, or were ignored. Fewer than one in 10 potential cryptocurrency buyers were aware of consumer warnings on the [[Financial Conduct Authority]] (FCA) website, and 12% of crypto users were not aware that their holdings were not protected by [[Financial Services Compensation Scheme|statutory compensation]].<ref>{{cite web |work=Investment Week |first=Anna |last=Fedorova |date=17 June 2021 |title=FCA warns on UK crypto use increase despite gaps in understanding |url=https://www.investmentweek.co.uk/news/4033010/fca-warns-uk-crypto-increase-despite-gaps-understanding |access-date=9 May 2022 |archive-date=28 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220528071437/https://www.investmentweek.co.uk/news/4033010/fca-warns-uk-crypto-increase-despite-gaps-understanding |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |first=Joshua |last=Oliver |title=Most would-be crypto investors unaware of UK regulator's warnings |date=17 June 2021 |work=Financial Times |url=https://www.ft.com/content/39718cda-5cd1-4f0d-b7e3-0151e45bf25b |url-access=subscription |access-date=23 June 2021 |archive-date=24 June 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210624204500/https://www.ft.com/content/39718cda-5cd1-4f0d-b7e3-0151e45bf25b |url-status=live }}</ref> Of 1,000 respondents between the ages of eighteen and forty, 70% wrongly assumed cryptocurrencies were regulated, 75% of younger crypto investors claimed to be driven by competition with friends and family, and 58% said that social media enticed them to make high risk investments.<ref>{{cite web |last=Browne |first=Ryan |date=19 October 2021 |title=Most young crypto traders don't realize it's not regulated, UK markets watchdog says |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/10/19/young-traders-treat-crypto-investing-like-a-competition-fca-says.html |access-date=1 March 2022 |website=CNBC |language=en |archive-date=1 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220301121820/https://www.cnbc.com/2021/10/19/young-traders-treat-crypto-investing-like-a-competition-fca-says.html |url-status=live }}</ref> The FCA recommends making use of its warning list, which flags unauthorized financial firms.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.fca.org.uk/consumers/unauthorised-firms-individuals |title=Unauthorised firms and individuals |publisher=[[Financial Conduct Authority]] (FCA) |date=19 August 2021 |access-date=3 March 2022 |archive-date=3 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220303180513/https://www.fca.org.uk/consumers/unauthorised-firms-individuals |url-status=live }}</ref>

Many banks do not offer virtual currency services themselves and can refuse to do business with virtual currency companies.<ref>{{cite web |last=Sidel |first=Robin |date=22 December 2013 |title=Banks Mostly Avoid Providing Bitcoin Services. Lenders Don't Share Investors' Enthusiasm for the Virtual-Currency Craze |url=https://www.wsj.com/news/articles/SB10001424052702304202204579252850121034702 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151119021729/http://www.wsj.com/news/articles/SB10001424052702304202204579252850121034702 |archive-date=19 November 2015 |access-date=29 December 2013 |website=The Wall Street Journal}}</ref> In 2014, Gareth Murphy, a senior banking officer, suggested that the widespread adoption of cryptocurrencies may lead to too much money being [[Obfuscation|obfuscated]], blinding economists who would use such information to better steer the economy.<ref>{{Cite news |date=3 July 2014 |title=Central Bank official warns on Bitcoin impact |work=RTE |url=https://www.rte.ie/news/business/2014/0703/628309-bitfin-conference/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150209064737/http://www.rte.ie/news/business/2014/0703/628309-bitfin-conference/ |archive-date=9 February 2015}}</ref> While traditional financial products have strong consumer protections in place, there is no intermediary with the power to limit consumer losses if bitcoins are lost or stolen. One of the features cryptocurrency lacks in comparison to credit cards, for example, is consumer protection against fraud, such as [[chargeback]]s.{{Citation needed|date=December 2025}}

The French regulator [[Autorité des marchés financiers (France)|Autorité des marchés financiers]] (AMF) lists 16 websites of companies that solicit investment in cryptocurrency without being authorized to do so in France.<ref>{{cite web |title=Warnings and blacklists of unauthorized companies and websites: Forex, binary options, miscellaneous goods, crypto-assets derivatives, usurpations |url=https://www.amf-france.org/en/warnings/warnings-and-blacklists |access-date=2 March 2022 |website=AMF |language=en |archive-date=2 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220302135153/https://www.amf-france.org/en/warnings/warnings-and-blacklists |url-status=live }}</ref>

An October 2021 paper by the [[National Bureau of Economic Research]] found that bitcoin suffers from systemic risk as the top 10,000 addresses control about one-third of all bitcoin in circulation.<ref>{{cite magazine |title=Bitcoin Is Still Concentrated in a Few Hands, Study Finds |url=https://time.com/6110392/bitcoin-ownership/ |access-date=3 March 2022 |magazine=Time |language=en |archive-date=18 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240618032614/https://time.com/6110392/bitcoin-ownership/ |url-status=live }}</ref> It is even worse for miners, with 0.01% controlling 50% of the capacity. According to researcher Flipside Crypto, less than 2% of anonymous accounts control 95% of all available bitcoin supply.<ref>{{cite web |title=Bitcoin's price just passed a huge milestone |url=https://fortune.com/2021/01/07/bitcoin-price-today-soars-ether-cryptocurrency-marketcap/ |access-date=3 March 2022 |website=Fortune |language=en |archive-date=3 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220303161428/https://fortune.com/2021/01/07/bitcoin-price-today-soars-ether-cryptocurrency-marketcap/ |url-status=live }}</ref> This is considered risky as a great deal of the market is in the hands of a few entities.{{Citation needed|date=December 2025}}

A paper by John Griffin, a finance professor at the [[University of Texas at Austin|University of Texas]], and Amin Shams, a graduate student, found that in 2017 the price of bitcoin had been substantially inflated using another cryptocurrency, Tether.<ref>{{cite web |last=Popper |first=Nathaniel |date=13 June 2018 |title=Bitcoin's Price Was Artificially Inflated Last Year, Researchers Say |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2018/06/13/bitcoins-price-was-artificially-inflated-last-year-researchers-say.html |access-date=3 March 2022 |website=CNBC |language=en |archive-date=3 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220303123437/https://www.cnbc.com/2018/06/13/bitcoins-price-was-artificially-inflated-last-year-researchers-say.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Roger Lowenstein]], author of "''Bank of America: The Epic Struggle to Create the Federal Reserve,''" said in a 2022 New York Times story that [[FTX]] currency exchange will face over $8 billion in claims.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Lowenstein |first=Roger |date=12 November 2022 |title=FTX's founder was called a modern-day J.P. Morgan. The analogy still works. |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/11/12/business/dealbook/ftx-bankman-fried-central-banks.html |access-date=13 November 2022 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=13 November 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221113051328/https://www.nytimes.com/2022/11/12/business/dealbook/ftx-bankman-fried-central-banks.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Non-fungible tokens===
[[Non-fungible token]]s (NFTs) are digital assets that represent art, collectibles, gaming, etc. Like crypto, their data is stored on the blockchain. NFTs are bought and traded using cryptocurrency. The Ethereum blockchain was the first place where NFTs were implemented, but now many other blockchains have created their own versions of NFTs.

===Banks===
{{See also|2023 United States banking crisis}}

According to Vanessa Grellet, renowned panelist in blockchain conferences,<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.forbes.fr/technologie/etat-des-lieux-des-nft-au-paris-blockchain-week-summit/ |title=État des lieux des NFT au Paris Blockchain Week Summit |first=Frédéric |last=Bonelli |language=French |access-date=26 September 2024 |website=Forbes |date=21 May 2019}}</ref> there was an increasing interest from traditional [[stock exchange]]s in crypto-assets at the end of the 2010s, while crypto-exchanges such as [[Coinbase]] were gradually entering the traditional [[financial market]]s. This convergence marked a significant trend where conventional financial actors were adopting blockchain technology to enhance operational efficiency, while the crypto world introduced innovations like [[Security token offering|Security Token Offering]] (STO), enabling new ways of [[fundraising]]. Tokenization, turning assets such as [[real estate]], [[investment fund]]s, and [[private equity]] into blockchain-based tokens, had the potential to make traditionally illiquid assets more accessible to investors. Despite the regulatory risks associated with such developments, major financial institutions, including [[JPMorgan Chase]], were actively working on blockchain initiatives, exemplified by the creation of Quorum, a private blockchain platform.<ref name=LT>{{cite news |url=https://www.latribune.fr/entreprises-finance/banques-finance/les-bourses-traditionnelles-vont-s-interesser-aux-crypto-actifs-et-vice-versa-vanessa-grellet-consensys-817978.html |title=Les Bourses traditionnelles vont s'intéresser aux crypto-actifs et vice-versa |last=Cuny |first=Delphine |website=La Tribune |language=French |date=23 May 2019 |access-date=29 September 2024}}</ref>

As the first big Wall Street bank to embrace cryptocurrencies, [[Morgan Stanley]] announced on 17 March 2021 that they will be offering access to bitcoin funds for their wealthy clients through three funds which enable bitcoin ownership for investors with an aggressive risk tolerance.<ref>{{cite web|last=Son|first=Hugh|date=17 March 2021|title=Morgan Stanley becomes the first big U.S. bank to offer its wealthy clients access to bitcoin funds|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/03/17/bitcoin-morgan-stanley-is-the-first-big-us-bank-to-offer-wealthy-clients-access-to-bitcoin-funds.html|access-date=1 August 2021|website=CNBC|language=en|archive-date=1 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210801153726/https://www.cnbc.com/2021/03/17/bitcoin-morgan-stanley-is-the-first-big-us-bank-to-offer-wealthy-clients-access-to-bitcoin-funds.html|url-status=live}}</ref> BNY Mellon on 11 February 2021 announced that it would begin offering cryptocurrency services to its clients.<ref>{{cite web|last=Franck|first=Thomas|date=11 February 2021|title=BNY Mellon to offer bitcoin services, a validation of crypto from a key bank in the financial system|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/02/11/bny-mellon-to-offer-bitcoin-services-a-validation-of-crypto-from-a-key-bank-in-the-financial-system.html|access-date=1 August 2021|website=CNBC|language=en|archive-date=1 August 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210801153726/https://www.cnbc.com/2021/02/11/bny-mellon-to-offer-bitcoin-services-a-validation-of-crypto-from-a-key-bank-in-the-financial-system.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

On 20 April 2021,<ref>{{cite web |date=20 April 2021 |title=Venmo adds support for buying, holding and selling cryptocurrencies |url=https://techcrunch.com/2021/04/20/venmo-adds-support-for-buying-holding-and-selling-cryptocurrencies/ |access-date=1 August 2021 |website=TechCrunch |language=en-US |archive-date=1 August 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210801155827/https://techcrunch.com/2021/04/20/venmo-adds-support-for-buying-holding-and-selling-cryptocurrencies/ |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Venmo]] added support to its platform to enable customers to buy, hold and sell cryptocurrencies.<ref>{{cite web|title=Buying Cryptocurrency on Venmo|url=https://help.venmo.com/hc/en-us/articles/360061922654-Buying-Cryptocurrency-on-Venmo-|access-date=1 August 2021|website=Venmo|language=en-US|archive-date=31 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210731194526/https://help.venmo.com/hc/en-us/articles/360061922654-Buying-Cryptocurrency-on-Venmo-|url-status=live}}</ref>

In October 2021, financial services company [[Mastercard]] announced it is working with digital asset manager [[Bakkt]] on a platform that would allow any bank or merchant on the Mastercard network to offer cryptocurrency services.<ref>{{cite web|last=Son|first=Hugh|date=25 October 2021|title=Mastercard says any bank or merchant on its vast network can soon offer crypto services|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2021/10/25/mastercard-says-any-bank-or-merchant-on-its-vast-network-can-soon-offer-crypto-services.html|access-date=29 November 2021|website=CNBC|language=en|archive-date=28 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211128164748/https://www.cnbc.com/2021/10/25/mastercard-says-any-bank-or-merchant-on-its-vast-network-can-soon-offer-crypto-services.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Environmental effects===
{{See also|Environmental impact of bitcoin}}

Mining for [[proof-of-work]] (PoW) cryptocurrencies requires enormous amounts of electricity and consequently comes with a large [[carbon footprint]] due to causing [[greenhouse gas emissions]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Foteinis|first=Spyros|date=7 February 2018|title=Bitcoin's alarming carbon footprint|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=554|issue=7691|page=169|doi=10.1038/d41586-018-01625-x|bibcode=2018Natur.554..169F|doi-access=free}}</ref> Proof-of-work blockchains such as bitcoin, [[Ethereum]], [[Litecoin]], and [[Monero]] were estimated to have added between 3 million and 15 million tons of [[Carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere|carbon dioxide ({{CO2}}) to the atmosphere]] in the period from 1 January 2016 to 30 June 2017.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Krause |first1=Max J. |last2=Tolaymat |first2=Thabet |title=Quantification of energy and carbon costs for mining cryptocurrencies |journal=Nature Sustainability |date=November 2018 |volume=1 |issue=11 |pages=711–718 |doi=10.1038/s41893-018-0152-7 |bibcode=2018NatSu...1..711K |s2cid=169170289 }}</ref> By November 2018, bitcoin was estimated to have an annual [[energy consumption]] of 45.8TWh, generating 22.0 to 22.9 million tons of {{CO2}}, rivalling nations like [[Jordan]] and [[Sri Lanka]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Stoll |first1=Christian |last2=Klaaßen |first2=Lena |last3=Gallersdörfer |first3=Ulrich |title=The Carbon Footprint of Bitcoin |journal=Joule |date=July 2019 |volume=3 |issue=7 |pages=1647–1661 |doi=10.1016/j.joule.2019.05.012 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2019Joule...3.1647S }}</ref> By the end of 2021, bitcoin was estimated to produce 65.4 million tons of {{CO2}}, as much as [[Greece]],<ref>{{cite web |last=Davies |first=Pascale |date=26 February 2022 |title=Bitcoin mining is worse for the environment now since China banned it |url=https://www.euronews.com/next/2022/02/26/bitcoin-mining-was-actually-worse-for-the-environment-since-china-banned-it-a-new-study-sa |access-date=1 March 2022 |website=euronews |language=en |archive-date=1 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220301145948/https://www.euronews.com/next/2022/02/26/bitcoin-mining-was-actually-worse-for-the-environment-since-china-banned-it-a-new-study-sa |url-status=live }}</ref> and consume between 91 and 177 terawatt-hours annually.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Huang |first1=Jon |last2=O'Neill |first2=Claire |last3=Tabuchi |first3=Hiroko |author-link=Hiroko Tabuchi |date=3 September 2021 |title=Bitcoin Uses More Electricity Than Many Countries. How Is That Possible? |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2021/09/03/climate/bitcoin-carbon-footprint-electricity.html |access-date=1 March 2022 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=17 February 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230217105559/https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2021/09/03/climate/bitcoin-carbon-footprint-electricity.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Bitcoin energy consumption worldwide 2017-2021 |url=https://www.statista.com/statistics/881472/worldwide-bitcoin-energy-consumption/ |access-date=1 March 2022 |website=Statista |language=en |archive-date=1 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220301145404/https://www.statista.com/statistics/881472/worldwide-bitcoin-energy-consumption/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Critics have also identified a large [[electronic waste]] problem in disposing of [[Bitcoin mining|mining rigs]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=de Vries |first1=Alex |title=Renewable Energy Will Not Solve Bitcoin's Sustainability Problem |journal=Joule |date=April 2019 |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=893–898 |doi=10.1016/j.joule.2019.02.007 |s2cid=169784459 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2019Joule...3..893D }}</ref> Mining hardware is improving at a fast rate, quickly resulting in older generations of hardware.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Livni|first=Ephrat|date=11 October 2021|title=Can Crypto Go Green?|work=[[The New York Times]]|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/10/10/business/dealbook/crypto-climate.html|access-date=23 January 2022|archive-date=22 January 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220122074143/https://www.nytimes.com/2021/10/10/business/dealbook/crypto-climate.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

Bitcoin is the least energy-efficient cryptocurrency, using 707.6 kilowatt-hours of electricity per transaction.<ref>{{cite web|last=Ponciano|first=Jonathan|title=Bill Gates Sounds Alarm On Bitcoin's Energy Consumption–Here's Why Crypto Is Bad For Climate Change|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/jonathanponciano/2021/03/09/bill-gates-bitcoin-crypto-climate-change/|access-date=30 July 2021|website=Forbes|language=en|archive-date=11 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210711110650/https://www.forbes.com/sites/jonathanponciano/2021/03/09/bill-gates-bitcoin-crypto-climate-change/|url-status=live}}</ref>

Before June 2021, China was the primary location for bitcoin mining. However, due to concerns over power usage and other factors, China forced out bitcoin operations, at least temporarily. As a result, the United States promptly emerged as the top global leader in the industry. An example of a gross amount of electronic waste associated with bitcoin mining operations in the US is a facility located in Dalton, Georgia which is consuming nearly the same amount of electricity as the combined power usage of 97,000 households in its vicinity. Another example is that Riot Platforms operates a bitcoin mining facility in Rockdale, Texas, which consumes approximately as much electricity as the nearby 300,000 households. This makes it the most energy-intensive bitcoin mining operation in the United States.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Dance |first1=Gabriel J. X. |last2=Wallace |first2=Tim |last3=Levitt |first3=Zach |date=10 April 2023 |title=The Real-World Costs of the Digital Race for Bitcoin |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/04/09/business/bitcoin-mining-electricity-pollution.html |access-date=14 April 2023 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=10 April 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230410164020/https://www.nytimes.com/2023/04/09/business/bitcoin-mining-electricity-pollution.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

The world's second-largest cryptocurrency, Ethereum, uses 62.56 kilowatt-hours of electricity per transaction.<ref>{{cite web|last=Harper|first=Chris|date=13 May 2021|title=The most energy efficient cryptocurrency after Tesla axed Bitcoin|url=https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/news/uk-news/what-most-energy-efficient-cryptocurrency-20588731|access-date=30 July 2021|website=BirminghamLive|language=en|archive-date=13 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210713214357/https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/news/uk-news/what-most-energy-efficient-cryptocurrency-20588731|url-status=live}}</ref> [[XRP]] is the world's most energy efficient cryptocurrency, using 0.0079 kilowatt-hours of electricity per transaction.<ref name="laptopmag">{{cite web|last=Gedeon|first=Kimberly|date=1 June 2021|title=The most energy-efficient cryptocurrencies — Tesla's top picks to replace Bitcoin|url=https://www.laptopmag.com/uk/best-picks/most-energy-efficient-cryptocurrencies-the-best-picks-for-teslas-new-coin|access-date=30 July 2021|website=LaptopMag|language=en|archive-date=30 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210730143102/https://www.laptopmag.com/uk/best-picks/most-energy-efficient-cryptocurrencies-the-best-picks-for-teslas-new-coin|url-status=live}}</ref>

Although the biggest PoW blockchains consume energy on the scale of medium-sized countries, the annual power demand from [[Proof of stake|proof-of-stake]] (PoS) blockchains is on a scale equivalent to a housing estate. ''The Times'' identified six "environmentally friendly" cryptocurrencies: Bitgreen, [[Cardano (blockchain platform)|Cardano]], [[Chia (cryptocurrency)|Chia]], [[IOTA (technology)|IOTA]], [[Nano (cryptocurrency)|Nano]], and Solarcoin.<ref>{{cite web |first=Rachel |last=Lacey |date=1 March 2022 |title=Everything you need to know about eco-friendly cryptocurrencies |work=[[The Times]] |url=https://www.thetimes.co.uk/money-mentor/article/eco-friendly-cryptocurrencies/ |access-date=9 May 2022 |archive-date=8 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220508232743/https://www.thetimes.co.uk/money-mentor/article/eco-friendly-cryptocurrencies/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Academics and researchers have used various methods for estimating the energy use and energy efficiency of blockchains. A study of the six largest PoS networks in May 2021 concluded:
* [[Cardano (blockchain platform)|Cardano]] has the lowest electricity use per node;
* [[Polkadot (cryptocurrency)|Polkadot]] has the lowest electricity use overall; and
* [[Solana (blockchain platform)|Solana]] has the lowest electricity use per transaction.

In terms of annual consumption (kWh/year), the figures were: Polkadot (70,237), [[Tezos]] (113,249), [[Avalanche (blockchain platform)|Avalanche]] (489,311), [[Algorand]] (512,671), Cardano (598,755) and Solana (1,967,930). This equates to Polkadot consuming 7 times the electricity of an average U.S. home, Cardano 57 homes and Solana 200 times as much. The research concluded that PoS networks consumed 0.001% the electricity of the bitcoin network.<ref>{{cite web |first=Joanna |last=Ossinger |title=Polkadot Has Least Carbon Footprint, Crypto Researcher Says |work=Bloomberg |date=2 February 2022 |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-02-02/polkadot-has-smallest-carbon-footprint-crypto-researcher-says |access-date=9 May 2022 |archive-date=12 April 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220412172017/https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2022-02-02/polkadot-has-smallest-carbon-footprint-crypto-researcher-says |url-status=live }}</ref> University College London researchers reached a similar conclusion.<ref>{{cite web |first=Jonathan |last=Spencer Jones |date=13 September 2021 |title=Proof-of-stake blockchains – not all are equal |work=Smart Energy International |url=https://www.smart-energy.com/industry-sectors/new-technology/proof-of-stake-blockchains-not-all-are-equal/ |access-date=9 May 2022 |archive-date=25 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210925061707/https://www.smart-energy.com/industry-sectors/new-technology/proof-of-stake-blockchains-not-all-are-equal/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Some studies have modeled Bitcoin mining as a potentially flexible electricity load, suggesting that, under certain conditions, mining operations could use otherwise curtailed electricity or improve project economics.<ref name="Fridgen2021">{{Cite journal|last1=Fridgen|first1=Gilbert|last2=Körner|first2=Marc-Fabian|last3=Walters|first3=Steffen|last4=Weibelzahl|first4=Martin|date=9 March 2021|title=Not All Doom and Gloom: How Energy-Intensive and Temporally Flexible Data Center Applications May Actually Promote Renewable Energy Sources|journal=Business & Information Systems Engineering|language=en|volume=63|issue=3|pages=243–256|doi=10.1007/s12599-021-00686-z|s2cid=233664180|issn=2363-7005|quote=To gain applicable knowledge, this paper evaluates the developed model by means of two use-cases with real-world data, namely AWS computing instances for training Machine Learning algorithms and Bitcoin mining as relevant DC applications. The results illustrate that for both cases the NPV of the IES compared to a stand-alone RES-plant increases, which may lead to a promotion of RES-plants.|doi-access=free|hdl=10419/287421|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Dajani |first=Mona E. |date=26 April 2021 |title=Green Bitcoin Does Not Have to Be an Oxymoron |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/environment-and-energy/green-bitcoin-does-not-have-to-be-an-oxymoron |access-date=16 January 2022 |website=news.bloomberglaw.com |language=en |quote=One way to invest in Bitcoin that has a positive effect on renewable energy is to encourage mining operations near wind or solar sites. This provides a customer for power that might otherwise need to be transmitted or stored, saving money as well as carbon. |archive-date=16 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220116122337/https://news.bloomberglaw.com/environment-and-energy/green-bitcoin-does-not-have-to-be-an-oxymoron |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Eid|first1=Bilal|last2=Islam|first2=Md Rabiul|last3=Shah|first3=Rakibuzzaman|last4=Nahid|first4=Abdullah-Al|last5=Kouzani|first5=Abbas Z.|last6=Mahmud|first6=M. A. Parvez|date=1 November 2021|title=Enhanced Profitability of Photovoltaic Plants By Utilizing Cryptocurrency-Based Mining Load|journal=IEEE Transactions on Applied Superconductivity|volume=31|issue=8|pages=1–5|doi=10.1109/TASC.2021.3096503|bibcode=2021ITAS...3196503E|hdl=20.500.11782/2513|s2cid=237245955|issn=1558-2515|quote=The grid connected photovoltaic (PV) power plants (PVPPs) are booming nowadays. The main problem facing the PV power plants deployment is the intermittency which leads to instability of the grid. [...] This paper investigating the usage of a customized load - cryptocurrency mining rig - to create an added value for the owner of the plant and increase the ROI of the project. [...] The developed strategy is able to keep the profitability as high as possible during the fluctuation of the mining network.|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bastian-Pinto |first1=Carlos L. |last2=Araujo |first2=Felipe V. de S. |last3=Brandão |first3=Luiz E. |last4=Gomes |first4=Leonardo L. |title=Hedging renewable energy investments with Bitcoin mining |journal=Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews |date=March 2021 |volume=138 |article-number=110520 |doi=10.1016/j.rser.2020.110520 |bibcode=2021RSERv.13810520B |quote=Windfarms can hedge electricity price risk by investing in Bitcoin mining. [...] These findings, which can also be applied to other renewable energy sources, may be of interest to both the energy generator as well as the system regulator as it creates an incentive for early investment in sustainable and renewable energy sources. }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rennie |first1=Ellie |title=Climate Change and the Legitimacy of Bitcoin: Legitimacy and Delegitimisation in Relation to Distributed Ledgers |journal=Cryptoeconomic Systems |date=22 April 2024 |volume=3 |issue=1 |doi=10.21428/58320208.d891046f }}</ref>

===Technological limitations===
There are also purely technical elements in play. For example, technological advancement in cryptocurrencies such as bitcoin result in high up-front costs to miners in the form of specialized [[computer hardware|hardware]] and [[software]].<ref>[https://theweek.com/article/index/242753/want-to-make-money-off-bitcoin-mining-hint-dont-mine Want to make money off Bitcoin mining? Hint: Don't mine] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140505181855/http://theweek.com/article/index/242753/want-to-make-money-off-bitcoin-mining-hint-dont-mine |date=5 May 2014 }}, ''The Week'', 15 April 2013</ref> Cryptocurrency transactions are normally irreversible after a number of blocks confirm the transaction. Additionally, cryptocurrency private keys can be permanently lost from local storage due to malware, data loss, or simply carelessness. This precludes the cryptocurrency from any usage whatsoever, permanently, thus removing it from the market.<ref>[http://c4ss.org/content/25638 Keeping Your Cryptocurrency Safe] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140712235229/http://c4ss.org/content/25638 |date=12 July 2014 }}, Center for a Stateless Society, 1 April 2014</ref>

===Academic studies===
{{Main|Ledger (journal)}}

In September 2015, the establishment of the [[peer-reviewed]] [[academic journal]] ''[[Ledger (journal)|Ledger]]'' ({{ISSN|2379-5980}}) was announced. It covers studies of cryptocurrencies and related technologies, and is published by the [[University of Pittsburgh]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Hertig |first=Alyssa |date=15 September 2015 |title=Introducing Ledger, the First Bitcoin-Only Academic Journal |url=https://www.vice.com/en/article/introducing-ledger-the-first-bitcoin-only-academic-journal/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170110172807/http://motherboard.vice.com/read/introducing-ledger-the-first-bitcoin-only-academic-journal |archive-date=10 January 2017 |website=Motherboard}}</ref>

The journal encourages authors to [[Digital signature|digitally sign]] a [[Hash function|file hash]] of submitted papers, which will then be [[Trusted timestamping|timestamped]] into the bitcoin [[Blockchain (database)|blockchain]]. Authors are also asked to include a personal bitcoin address in the first page of their papers.<ref>{{cite web |title=Editorial Policies |url=http://ledgerjournal.org/ojs/index.php/ledger/about/editorialPolicies#custom-0 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161223135741/http://www.ledgerjournal.org/ojs/index.php/ledger/about/editorialPolicies#custom-0 |archive-date=23 December 2016 |access-date=24 September 2015 |website=ledgerjournal.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rizun |first1=Peter R. |last2=Wilmer |first2=Christopher E. |last3=Burley |first3=Richard Ford |last4=Miller |first4=Andrew |year=2015 |title=How to Write and Format an Article for Ledger |journal=[[Ledger (journal)|Ledger]] |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=1–12 |url=http://ledger.pitt.edu/ojs/public/journals/1/AuthorGuide.pdf |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150922190603/http://ledger.pitt.edu/ojs/public/journals/1/AuthorGuide.pdf |archive-date=22 September 2015}}</ref>

===Aid agencies===
A number of [[Aid agency|aid agencies]] have started accepting donations in cryptocurrencies, including [[UNICEF]].<ref name="ibtimesunicef">{{Cite news |last=Mendoza |first=Ron |date=14 October 2019 |title=UNICEF Blockchain Fund: First UN organization To Accept Cryptocurrency Donations |work=IB Times |url=https://www.ibtimes.com/unicef-blockchain-fund-first-un-organization-accept-cryptocurrency-donations-2845332 |access-date=14 October 2019 |archive-date=14 October 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191014071136/https://www.ibtimes.com/unicef-blockchain-fund-first-un-organization-accept-cryptocurrency-donations-2845332 |url-status=live }}</ref> Christopher Fabian, principal adviser at UNICEF Innovation, said the children's fund would uphold donor protocols, meaning that people making donations online would have to pass checks before they were allowed to deposit funds.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.unicef.org/press-releases/unicef-launches-cryptocurrency-fund|title=UNICEF launches Cryptocurrency Fund|date=9 October 2019|website=www.unicef.org|access-date=1 November 2019|archive-date=2 November 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191102011325/https://www.unicef.org/press-releases/unicef-launches-cryptocurrency-fund|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Doshi |first=Vidhi |date=9 October 2019 |title=Unicef now accepting donations through bitcoin and ether |work=The Guardian |url=http://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2019/oct/09/unicef-now-accepting-donations-through-bitcoin-and-ether |access-date=22 October 2020 |archive-date=28 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201028034637/https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2019/oct/09/unicef-now-accepting-donations-through-bitcoin-and-ether |url-status=live }}</ref>

However, in 2021, there was a backlash against donations in bitcoin because of the environmental emissions it caused. Some agencies stopped accepting bitcoin and others turned to "greener" cryptocurrencies.<ref>{{cite web |first=Allison |last=Murray |date=2 March 2022 |title=Charities are turning to bitcoin and NFTs to raise money. Not everyone thinks it's a great idea |work=ZDNet |url=https://www.zdnet.com/finance/blockchain/charities-are-turning-to-cryptocurrencies-and-nfts-not-everyone-thinks-its-a-great-idea/ |access-date=9 May 2022 |archive-date=12 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220512070349/https://www.zdnet.com/finance/blockchain/charities-are-turning-to-cryptocurrencies-and-nfts-not-everyone-thinks-its-a-great-idea/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The [[Greenpeace USA|U.S. arm of Greenpeace]] stopped accepting bitcoin donations after seven years. It said: "As the amount of energy needed to run bitcoin became clearer, this policy became no longer tenable."<ref>{{cite web |first1=Katie |last1=Martin |first2=Billy |last2=Nauman |date=20 May 2021 |title=Bitcoin's growing energy problem: 'It's a dirty currency' |work=Financial Times |url=https://www.ft.com/content/1aecb2db-8f61-427c-a413-3b929291c8ac |access-date=8 February 2022 |archive-date=9 February 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220209142620/https://www.ft.com/content/1aecb2db-8f61-427c-a413-3b929291c8ac |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2022, the [[Ukrainian government]] raised over {{Currency|10 million|USD}} worth of aid through cryptocurrency following the [[2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Browne |first1=Ryan |title=Ukraine government raises over $10 million in cryptocurrency donations |url=https://www.cnbc.com/2022/02/27/ukraine-government-raises-over-10-million-in-cryptocurrency-donations.html |access-date=27 February 2022 |work=CNBC |date=27 February 2022 |archive-date=25 March 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220325115433/https://www.cnbc.com/2022/02/27/ukraine-government-raises-over-10-million-in-cryptocurrency-donations.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Investors [[Warren Buffett]] and [[George Soros]] have respectively characterized it in 2014–2018 as a "mirage"<ref>{{cite web |last=Crippen |first=Alex |date=14 March 2014 |title=Bitcoin? |website=CNBC }}</ref> and a "bubble".<ref name="GnMSoros">{{cite news |last1=Porzecanski |first1=Katia |date=25 January 2018 |title=George Soros: Bitcoin is a bubble, Trump is a 'danger to the world' |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/globe-investor/investment-ideas/george-soros-says-bitcoin-bubble-wont-have-sharp-break-like-others/article37739168/ |url-status=live |access-date=7 June 2018
